title: Selective Layer Freezing via Gradient Sensitivity Analysis for VLA Knowledge Preservation
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs currently relies on architectural interventions (e.g., frozen backbone layers or adapter modules) applied uniformly, without accounting for which specific layers actually encode task-relevant semantic knowledge versus low-level visual features. Uniform insulation may over-constrain learning in layers that benefit from fine-tuning, or under-protect layers most critical to generalization.

Proposed Method: We introduce Gradient Sensitivity-Guided Insulation (GSGI), a data-driven technique that dynamically identifies which VLM backbone layers to insulate during VLA training. Before fine-tuning, we compute per-layer Fisher Information scores on a held-out semantic benchmark (e.g., VQA or captioning tasks) to quantify each layer's contribution to semantic knowledge. Layers with high Fisher scores are selectively frozen or equipped with lightweight LoRA adapters, while layers with low scores are allowed full gradient updates. The insulation schedule can also adapt during training as gradient norms shift.

Experiments: (1) Compare GSGI against full fine-tuning, uniform freezing, and the knowledge insulation baseline from the anchor paper on manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO, OpenVLA-OFT); (2) Measure semantic knowledge retention via VQA and zero-shot captioning probes throughout training; (3) Evaluate generalization to novel objects/instructions; (4) Ablate Fisher threshold sensitivity and LoRA rank choices; (5) Measure wall-clock training speed and inference latency.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Models: When and Where to Insulate During Continual Robot Skill Acquisition
description:
Problem: While knowledge insulation prevents VLM backbone degradation during initial VLA training, robots must continuously acquire new skills post-deployment without catastrophically forgetting prior capabilities or losing VLM semantic knowledge. The optimal insulation strategy likely changes across continual learning phases, but no principled method exists for dynamically adjusting which layers to protect versus fine-tune.

Proposed Method: We propose Adaptive Insulation Scheduling (AIS), which monitors layer-wise Fisher information and gradient signal-to-noise ratios during continual skill acquisition to dynamically determine per-layer insulation boundaries. Early semantic layers receive stronger insulation as new skills are added, while later cross-modal fusion layers are selectively unfrozen when novel skills require new visual-semantic grounding. We introduce a lightweight 'semantic probe' that continuously evaluates VLM knowledge retention on held-out VQA tasks during robot training, using degradation signals to trigger insulation adjustments.

Experiments: (1) Continual skill acquisition benchmark on LIBERO and RoboSuite with 10+ sequential tasks; (2) Ablations comparing static vs. adaptive insulation schedules; (3) Semantic retention measured via VQA accuracy throughout training; (4) Real-robot experiments on a Franka arm learning 5 sequential manipulation skills; (5) Comparison against EWC, PackNet, and LoRA-based continual learning baselines on both task success rate and semantic knowledge retention metrics.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLA models treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect uniformly, but different layers encode different levels of semantic abstraction. When adapting to diverse robot morphologies (manipulators, quadrupeds, humanoids), blindly insulating all backbone layers may over-constrain task-specific adaptation or under-protect critical semantic representations. We lack principled methods for deciding *which* layers to insulate versus fine-tune per embodiment type.

Proposed Method: We introduce Morphology-Adaptive Selective Insulation (MASI), a method that uses gradient sensitivity analysis and representational similarity metrics (CKA) to automatically identify which VLM layers contain transferable semantic knowledge versus task-specific control signals for each robot morphology. MASI learns a binary insulation mask per layer through a bilevel optimization: the outer loop maximizes downstream task performance while the inner loop preserves VLM knowledge probing accuracy on held-out vision-language tasks.

Experiments: (1) Compare MASI against uniform insulation and full fine-tuning across three robot morphologies (arm, quadruped, dexterous hand) on standard manipulation benchmarks; (2) Measure semantic knowledge retention via VQA probing throughout training; (3) Ablate mask granularity (per-layer vs. per-attention-head); (4) Evaluate zero-shot transfer to unseen tasks as a function of insulation patterns learned per morphology.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge During Multi-Task Robot Policy Updates
description: Problem: VLA models deployed in the real world must continually adapt to new tasks and environments without catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired semantic knowledge or motor skills. Current knowledge insulation techniques (e.g., backbone freezing during initial VLA training) are static—they don't address the ongoing challenge of updating deployed policies as robots encounter novel tasks. Proposed Method: We introduce Gradient-Guided Semantic Preservation (GGSP), a continual learning framework that dynamically identifies and selectively freezes VLM backbone layers based on their semantic knowledge contribution (measured via representational similarity analysis against a frozen VLM reference) during each new task adaptation cycle. Unlike static insulation, GGSP applies layer-wise learning rate scaling inversely proportional to each layer's semantic drift, while allowing action expert modules to update freely. We additionally propose a semantic anchor replay buffer that periodically re-exposes the backbone to VLM pretraining exemplars to counteract gradual semantic erosion across sequential task updates. Experiments: We evaluate on a continual robot learning benchmark spanning 20 sequential manipulation tasks using simulated (RLBench) and real robot platforms, measuring (1) forward transfer to new tasks, (2) backward transfer/forgetting on old tasks, (3) semantic knowledge retention via VQA probing, and (4) inference latency overhead compared to static insulation baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Models: When and Where to Insulate During Continual Robot Skill Acquisition
description: Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs addresses catastrophic forgetting during initial VLA training, but real-world robot deployment requires continual learning of new skills post-deployment. When fine-tuning a deployed VLA on new tasks (e.g., new objects, environments, or manipulation primitives), the insulation strategy developed for initial training may be suboptimal — different VLM layers encode different semantic abstractions, and indiscriminately freezing all layers during skill updates may prevent necessary adaptation while over-updating others causes semantic degradation. Proposed Method: We develop a dynamic, layer-wise insulation curriculum for continual VLA fine-tuning. Using gradient signal-to-noise ratio and representational similarity analysis (CKA) across VLM layers, we automatically identify which layers have drifted from their pretrained semantic representations during each fine-tuning episode. We then apply selective LoRA-based updates only to layers that require task-specific adaptation while maintaining stronger insulation on layers with rich semantic content. A regularization term penalizes deviation from pretrained representations proportionally to each layer's measured semantic richness. Experiments: We evaluate on a continual manipulation benchmark with 20 sequential tasks using a Franka arm, measuring (1) forward transfer to new skills, (2) backward transfer/forgetting of previous skills, (3) VLM semantic benchmark retention (VQA, captioning), and (4) wall-clock training efficiency compared to full fine-tuning and uniform insulation baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Tasks
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone uniformly, applying the same insulation strategy regardless of task semantics or domain shift. However, different robot tasks (manipulation, navigation, dexterous grasping) require different degrees of semantic grounding versus motor specialization, suggesting that a fixed insulation strategy may over-constrain adaptation for tasks requiring novel visual concepts or under-protect knowledge for routine tasks. Method: We propose Task-Adaptive Selective Insulation (TASI), which dynamically determines per-layer and per-task insulation strength using a lightweight probing-based diagnostic. Before VLA fine-tuning, we run rapid linear probes on intermediate VLM layers to measure task-relevant semantic retention. Layers with high probe accuracy on task-relevant concepts receive stronger gradient isolation; layers encoding low-level features receive weaker insulation, permitting motor-relevant adaptation. We additionally propose a curriculum that relaxes insulation over training epochs as the action expert stabilizes. Experiments: We evaluate TASI on a diverse benchmark spanning 5 robot platforms (Franka, xArm, UR5, quadruped locomotion, mobile manipulation) using both in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization metrics. We compare against uniform insulation baselines from prior work, measuring VQA retention, task success rate, training wall-clock time, and sample efficiency across 50+ tasks to validate that adaptive insulation consistently outperforms one-size-fits-all approaches.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Manipulation Domains
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone uniformly, applying the same insulation strategy across all layers and task domains. However, different layers encode different levels of semantic abstraction, and different manipulation tasks (dexterous manipulation, long-horizon planning, contact-rich assembly) may benefit from varying degrees of backbone plasticity versus preservation. A one-size-fits-all insulation strategy may sacrifice task-relevant adaptation in lower semantic layers while still corrupting higher-level knowledge in upper layers.

Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-wise Adaptive Insulation (LAI), which learns per-layer insulation coefficients via a meta-gradient approach. During VLA fine-tuning, a lightweight auxiliary objective measures downstream semantic knowledge retention (via VQA probe tasks) per layer cluster, and gradient signals automatically tune how much each layer cluster is shielded from the action expert's influence. We additionally propose task-conditioned insulation gates that modulate insulation strength based on detected task complexity.

Experiments: (1) Ablation across insulation granularities (uniform vs. layer-group vs. per-layer) on LIBERO and FurnitureBench benchmarks; (2) Comparison against the baseline insulation technique from the anchor paper; (3) Transfer evaluation under distribution shift measuring both semantic VQA retention and policy success rate; (4) Analysis of learned insulation profiles across task families to reveal which layers benefit most from plasticity.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When Does Backbone Preservation Help vs. Hurt Cross-Domain Generalization?
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation prevents VLM backbone degradation during VLA training, but uniform insulation may be suboptimal—some VLM layers encode task-irrelevant priors that should be adapted for robotics (e.g., spatial reasoning, contact physics), while others encode semantic knowledge worth preserving. Determining which layers to insulate vs. fine-tune is an open problem.

Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Selective Knowledge Insulation (LSKI), a data-driven approach that quantifies per-layer 'semantic preservation scores' by measuring representational similarity (CKA) between pretrained and post-trained VLM activations on a held-out vision-language probe suite. Using these scores, we train a lightweight meta-policy that learns which layers to freeze, partially unfreeze, or fully fine-tune given a target robot domain, task complexity, and available demonstration budget. The meta-policy is trained via bilevel optimization: inner loop adapts VLA weights, outer loop maximizes downstream task success while penalizing semantic degradation.

Experiments: (1) Evaluate on diverse robot manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO, RLBench, real-world OpenX domains) across seen/unseen task categories; (2) Ablate freezing granularities (attention heads vs. full layers); (3) Compare against uniform insulation, full fine-tuning, and LoRA baselines; (4) Measure training wall-clock time, inference latency, and few-shot generalization to novel objects and instructions.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Tasks
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone uniformly, applying the same insulation strategy regardless of task complexity, embodiment, or semantic richness. However, different robot tasks demand different trade-offs between preserving VLM priors (e.g., object recognition for pick-and-place) and adapting representations for motor control (e.g., contact-rich manipulation). A single global insulation strategy may over-constrain adaptation for novel tasks or under-protect semantic knowledge for familiar ones.

Proposed Method: We introduce Task-Adaptive Selective Insulation (TASI), which learns per-layer insulation coefficients conditioned on task metadata (language description, embodiment type, training data volume). Rather than a fixed insulation mask, TASI uses a lightweight meta-network that predicts layer-wise LoRA scaling factors and gradient gates from task embeddings, allowing dynamic backbone protection. During training, we jointly optimize task performance and a knowledge retention objective measured via VQA probing benchmarks on held-out visual questions.

Experiments: We evaluate TASI on (1) OpenVLA and pi0-style architectures across 5 robot embodiments in simulation (LIBERO, FurnitureBench, RoboSuite), (2) few-shot generalization to novel objects/scenes, (3) semantic retention via VQA probing throughout training, and (4) ablations comparing global vs. selective insulation. We hypothesize TASI achieves better generalization-efficiency Pareto frontiers than uniform insulation.

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Training: When and Where to Insulate for Optimal Knowledge-Action Transfer
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, but different VLM layers encode qualitatively distinct knowledge (low-level visual features, mid-level spatial relations, high-level semantic concepts) that may benefit from different levels of coupling with the action expert during training. Naively freezing or insulating all layers uniformly may over-constrain action-relevant representations or under-protect semantically critical layers. Method: We propose Dynamic Selective Insulation (DSI), a training framework that learns per-layer, per-phase insulation schedules for VLA training. Using gradient similarity metrics between VLM backbone layers and the action expert loss, we identify which layers are being 'pulled away' from their pretrained representations and apply adaptive insulation coefficients accordingly. We introduce a curriculum that progressively relaxes insulation in lower layers as training stabilizes, while maintaining strong insulation in higher semantic layers. We also explore task-conditional insulation where the insulation strength adapts based on the semantic complexity of the instruction. Experiments: We evaluate on LIBERO, OpenVLA benchmarks, and real robot manipulation tasks measuring (1) zero-shot generalization to novel instructions, (2) training convergence speed, (3) layer-wise representational drift via CKA similarity, and (4) performance on interleaved language-action tasks requiring semantic grounding.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs has been studied primarily for a fixed robot embodiment and action space. However, deploying VLAs across heterogeneous robot morphologies (manipulators, quadrupeds, humanoids) requires understanding which VLM layers encode transferable semantic knowledge versus embodiment-specific priors—and whether uniform insulation strategies generalize across morphology shifts or whether layer-selective freezing schedules are needed. Naively applying the same insulation technique across morphologies may over-constrain adaptation for highly dissimilar embodiments or under-constrain it for similar ones.

Method: We propose Morphology-Adaptive Selective Insulation (MASI), which uses Fisher Information Matrix estimates computed on a small per-embodiment calibration dataset to rank VLM layers by their sensitivity to the new action space. Layers with low Fisher sensitivity are fully insulated; high-sensitivity layers receive partial insulation via a learned gating scalar. This produces a per-morphology insulation mask without full retraining.

Experiments: (1) Train a base VLA on a manipulator task suite, then adapt to quadruped locomotion, bimanual manipulation, and a humanoid whole-body task. (2) Compare MASI against full fine-tuning, uniform insulation, and LoRA baselines on task success, VLM knowledge retention (VQA benchmarks), and wall-clock training time. (3) Ablate Fisher threshold sensitivity and calibration dataset size to characterize the compute-performance tradeoff across morphology distance metrics.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for Heterogeneous VLA Adaptation: When to Insulate, When to Adapt
description:
Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs proposes insulating the VLM backbone uniformly during action expert training, but this one-size-fits-all approach may over-constrain task-specific adaptation in lower-level visual layers while under-protecting high-level semantic layers. Different VLM layers encode qualitatively different knowledge (low-level textures vs. high-level semantics), and the optimal insulation strategy likely varies by layer depth, task complexity, and domain shift magnitude.

Proposed Method: We introduce Gradient-Aware Selective Insulation (GASI), which dynamically determines per-layer insulation strength based on (1) the cosine similarity between backbone gradients induced by VLM pretraining objectives and VLA action objectives, and (2) the layer's measured semantic content via probing classifiers. Layers with high gradient conflict and high semantic content receive strong insulation; layers with aligned gradients and low semantic content remain adaptive. We implement this via learnable per-layer EWC-inspired penalties calibrated online during training.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) standard manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO, RLBench) measuring task success and VLM semantic retention probes, (2) cross-domain generalization (sim-to-real), and (3) few-shot adaptation to novel objects. We compare against uniform insulation, no insulation, and LoRA-based approaches, measuring training wall-clock time, semantic probe accuracy, and downstream task performance across varying dataset sizes.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Matters
description:
Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, applying uniform insulation strategies across all layers. However, different VLM layers encode qualitatively different knowledge (low-level visual features, mid-level semantic representations, high-level reasoning), and the optimal insulation strategy likely varies across layers and robot task types. Naively freezing everything may limit motor adaptation; freezing nothing corrupts semantic knowledge.

Proposed Method: We propose Layer-Adaptive Insulation (LAI), a method that learns per-layer insulation coefficients during VLA training. Each transformer layer receives a learnable gating scalar that interpolates between full gradient flow and complete insulation. We regularize these gates using a Fisher Information-based importance score computed from the original VLM's visual-language tasks, encouraging preservation of semantically critical layers while allowing task-relevant adaptation elsewhere. We also explore task-conditioned gating where insulation patterns adapt to whether tasks require language grounding versus visuomotor precision.

Experiments: (1) Analyze which VLM layers are most degraded by action expert integration using representation similarity analysis. (2) Compare LAI against uniform insulation and no-insulation baselines on LIBERO and OpenVLA benchmarks across language-conditioned manipulation tasks. (3) Measure training convergence speed, downstream VLM benchmark retention (VQA, captioning), and zero-shot generalization to novel instructions. (4) Ablate regularization strength and gate initialization strategies.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When to Insulate, When to Fine-tune
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone monolithically—either protecting all layers or none. However, different VLM layers encode different types of knowledge (low-level visual features, mid-level semantics, high-level reasoning), and robotic tasks may benefit from fine-tuning certain layers while preserving others. Naively insulating all layers may sacrifice task-specific adaptation; insulating none degrades semantic knowledge as shown in the anchor paper.

Proposed Method: We introduce Gradient-Informed Selective Insulation (GISI), a technique that identifies which VLM layers to freeze during VLA training based on layer-wise knowledge retention scores computed via Fisher information on a held-out VLM benchmark. Layers with high Fisher scores (critical for semantic knowledge) are insulated, while layers with low scores are allowed to adapt. We combine this with LoRA adapters on the insulated layers to enable lightweight task-specific tuning without catastrophic forgetting.

Experiments: (1) Compare GISI against full insulation, no insulation, and uniform LoRA on Open-X-Embodiment tasks measuring both control performance and VLM benchmark retention. (2) Ablate Fisher threshold values and LoRA rank. (3) Evaluate cross-task generalization on novel instruction following tasks. (4) Measure inference latency and training convergence speed. We expect GISI to achieve better control performance than full insulation while maintaining semantic knowledge better than no insulation.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Matters
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation paper treats VLM backbone protection as a binary or uniform choice, but different layers of a VLM encode qualitatively different knowledge—early layers capture low-level visual features while later layers encode high-level semantic and reasoning capabilities. Naively freezing or insulating all layers uniformly may over-constrain adaptation for motor-relevant representations while under-protecting task-critical semantic layers. Proposed Method: We develop a layer-wise adaptive insulation strategy that automatically identifies which transformer layers should be frozen, lightly regularized, or freely adapted during VLA training. We use gradient signal analysis and representational similarity (CKA) between pretrained VLM activations and fine-tuned VLA activations to construct a per-layer 'knowledge fragility score.' Layers with high fragility scores receive stronger insulation via EWC-style penalties or complete freezing, while motor-relevant intermediate layers receive light regularization. We also explore structured sparsity masks that allow selective neuron-level adaptation within otherwise insulated layers. Experiments: We evaluate on SimplerEnv and real robot manipulation benchmarks, measuring (1) downstream task success rate, (2) retained VQA and zero-shot generalization performance, (3) training convergence speed, and (4) robustness to novel object categories. We compare against uniform insulation baselines and ablate the fragility scoring function across multiple VLA backbone sizes (3B, 7B, 13B parameters).

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and What to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation technique demonstrates that protecting VLM backbone representations during VLA training improves semantic transfer and training speed. However, the optimal insulation strategy likely varies dramatically across robot morphologies (manipulators vs. bipeds vs. dexterous hands), action spaces (6-DOF vs. whole-body control), and task semantic complexity (language-conditioned manipulation vs. navigation). A uniform insulation recipe may leave performance on the table or cause negative transfer in heterogeneous deployment settings. Proposed Method: We introduce Morphology-Adaptive Knowledge Insulation (MAKI), which automatically determines per-layer freezing schedules by measuring representational drift (via centered kernel alignment, CKA) between the pretrained VLM and the fine-tuning trajectory. Layers whose representations drift beyond a learned threshold are selectively re-insulated via low-rank residual adapters (LoRA gates), while layers with stable representations remain fully frozen. A lightweight meta-controller learns the per-layer insulation policy across morphologies using gradient-based meta-learning on a small held-out semantic probing set. Experiments: We evaluate MAKI on three robot platforms (Franka arm, Unitree H1 biped, Shadow Hand), comparing against uniform insulation and full fine-tuning baselines. Metrics include task success rate, semantic probing accuracy (color/shape/spatial reasoning), training wall-clock time, and zero-shot generalization to novel object categories. Ablations examine sensitivity to CKA threshold, LoRA rank, and meta-training set size.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge Across Sequential Robot Task Acquisition
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation addresses VLM degradation during initial VLA training, robots must continuously acquire new manipulation skills over their deployment lifetime. Each new task risks catastrophic forgetting of both previously learned motor skills and the semantic knowledge inherited from VLM pretraining — creating a compound forgetting problem unique to VLAs. Proposed Method: We propose Semantic-Motor Decoupled Continual Learning (SMDCL), which identifies and selectively protects layer subsets responsible for semantic grounding versus motor control during sequential task training. Using gradient-based importance scoring (Fisher Information) computed separately on language-vision alignment objectives and action prediction objectives, we construct dynamic freeze masks that evolve as new tasks arrive. Crucially, we extend knowledge insulation principles by maintaining an 'insulation boundary' that shields VLM backbone layers from motor-task gradient interference across the entire task sequence, while allowing controlled plasticity in action expert parameters. We additionally introduce a semantic consistency replay mechanism using synthetic language-vision pairs generated by the frozen VLM itself as an anchor. Experiments: We evaluate on a sequential 10-task manipulation benchmark (MetaWorld + real robot), measuring (1) backward transfer on motor skills, (2) VLM semantic knowledge retention via VQA probing after each task, and (3) sample efficiency on new tasks, comparing against EWC, PackNet, and naive fine-tuning baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Models: When and What to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Embodiments
description:
Problem: While knowledge insulation techniques preserve VLM semantic knowledge during VLA training, current approaches apply uniform insulation strategies across all layers and training stages. Different VLM layers encode different levels of semantic abstraction (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantic concepts), and optimal insulation may vary depending on the target robot embodiment, task complexity, and available training data. A rigid insulation policy may over-constrain adaptation for novel embodiments while under-protecting critical semantic knowledge.

Proposed Method: We develop a dynamic, per-layer insulation scheduling framework that learns which VLM layers to freeze, partially update, or fully fine-tune at each training stage. We introduce a gradient-based 'semantic sensitivity score' that measures each layer's contribution to downstream language understanding benchmarks throughout VLA training. Using this score, we implement an adaptive insulation curriculum that progressively relaxes constraints on lower semantic-sensitivity layers while maintaining strict insulation on high-sensitivity layers. We further extend this to multi-embodiment training, learning embodiment-specific insulation masks shared across a common VLM backbone.

Experiments: (1) Ablations on insulation granularity using OpenVLA and π0 architectures across LIBERO, MetaWorld, and real robot manipulation tasks; (2) Zero-shot transfer to unseen embodiments comparing uniform vs. adaptive insulation; (3) Semantic retention evaluated via VQA benchmarks throughout training; (4) Training efficiency and wall-clock time comparisons.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, but different layers encode different levels of semantic abstraction. Low-level visual features may actually need updating for new robot embodiments (camera viewpoints, gripper morphologies), while high-level semantic layers should remain frozen. The optimal insulation strategy likely varies across robot types, task categories, and action spaces, yet current approaches apply uniform protection. Proposed Method: We introduce Morphology-Aware Selective Insulation (MASI), which learns per-layer insulation masks during a lightweight meta-adaptation phase. Specifically, we compute layer-wise 'semantic drift' scores by measuring representational similarity (CKA) between pretrained VLM activations and fine-tuned VLA activations across layers, then train a small gating network to predict which layers should be insulated given robot morphology embeddings and task descriptors. During VLA training, gates modulate gradient flow per layer rather than applying uniform backbone freezing. Experiments: We evaluate MASI on (1) cross-morphology transfer (arm→bimanual→mobile manipulation), (2) sim-to-real transfer on LIBERO and Open-X-Embodiment benchmarks, (3) training efficiency (steps to convergence) versus baseline knowledge insulation, and (4) semantic probe accuracy on VQA benchmarks post-adaptation. We hypothesize that selective insulation outperforms uniform approaches by 15-20% on novel morphology generalization while maintaining inference speed.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Models: When and Where to Insulate During Continual Robot Skill Acquisition
description:
Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs addresses catastrophic forgetting during initial VLA training, but robots deployed in the real world must continually acquire new skills without forgetting prior ones. Naive fine-tuning on new tasks degrades both VLM semantic knowledge and previously learned motor skills, yet full insulation prevents necessary adaptation. We need principled methods for deciding which layers to update when adding new robot skills post-deployment.

Proposed Method: We propose Skill-Adaptive Selective Insulation (SASI), a continual learning framework that dynamically determines per-layer update masks during new skill acquisition. Using Fisher Information computed over the action expert and VLM backbone jointly, we identify which parameters encode task-agnostic semantics vs. task-specific motor primitives. For each new skill, SASI freezes semantically critical layers (identified via Fisher overlap with VLM pretraining objectives), applies low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to motor-relevant layers, and maintains a small skill-specific parameter buffer. A knowledge retention score combining VQA accuracy and motor skill success rates guides the insulation boundary.

Experiments: (1) Sequential skill acquisition on FurnitureBench and LIBERO-90 across 10+ task sequences; (2) Ablations comparing full fine-tuning, full insulation, LoRA-only, and SASI; (3) Evaluation of VLM semantic retention via embodied QA benchmarks after each skill addition; (4) Real-robot experiments on a Franka arm learning 8 sequential manipulation tasks, measuring both forward transfer and backward interference.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When to Insulate, When to Fine-tune
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, applying uniform insulation across all layers. However, different transformer layers encode qualitatively different knowledge—early layers capture low-level visual features, middle layers encode compositional semantics, and later layers hold task-relevant reasoning. Blindly insulating all layers may unnecessarily restrict the adaptation of layers that genuinely benefit from robot-specific fine-tuning, while naively fine-tuning all layers destroys semantic knowledge as shown in the anchor paper. Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Adaptive Knowledge Insulation (LAKI), which computes per-layer 'knowledge sensitivity scores' during a brief probe phase using behavioral probing classifiers on a held-out semantic benchmark (e.g., VQA, spatial reasoning). Layers with high sensitivity scores are frozen or lightly regularized via EWC-style penalties, while layers with low sensitivity scores are fully fine-tuned. The action expert is coupled exclusively to the identified 'adaptation-safe' layers. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate on Open-X-Embodiment manipulation tasks comparing LAKI against full insulation, no insulation, and LoRA baselines; (2) Measure retention of semantic knowledge via VQA and spatial reasoning benchmarks throughout training; (3) Ablate sensitivity score computation methods; (4) Analyze convergence speed and generalization to novel object categories and instructions.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Fine-tuning: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Tasks
description: Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs demonstrates that protecting VLM backbone knowledge during action expert training improves generalization, but applies a uniform insulation strategy across all layers and tasks. Different robot manipulation tasks (e.g., language-conditioned grasping vs. long-horizon assembly) may benefit from different layer-wise insulation patterns — some tasks require deep semantic grounding while others prioritize low-level visuomotor features. Method: We propose Task-Adaptive Selective Insulation (TASI), which learns per-layer insulation coefficients conditioned on task embeddings. During VLA fine-tuning, a lightweight meta-network predicts which VLM layers to freeze, partially update, or fully fine-tune based on task semantic complexity scores derived from language instruction embeddings. We use gradient signal-to-noise ratio across layers as a differentiable proxy for beneficial knowledge transfer, allowing end-to-end optimization of the insulation policy. Experiments: We evaluate on a diverse suite of 20+ manipulation tasks in simulation (RLBench, LIBERO) and 8 real-robot tasks spanning varying semantic complexity. Metrics include training convergence speed, success rate on novel instructions, and catastrophic forgetting measured via VLM semantic benchmarks (VQA, captioning). Ablations compare uniform insulation, no insulation, full fine-tuning, and TASI variants to characterize when selective insulation matters most.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Training: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Tasks
description:
Problem: The knowledge insulation technique proposed for VLAs treats the VLM backbone uniformly, applying the same insulation strategy regardless of task semantics or robot embodiment. However, different manipulation tasks (e.g., language-conditioned grasping vs. long-horizon assembly) likely require different degrees of VLM backbone plasticity—rigid insulation may preserve knowledge but limit adaptation for tasks demanding novel visual-semantic grounding. We propose a task-adaptive, layer-selective insulation scheme that dynamically determines which VLM layers to freeze, partially update, or fully fine-tune based on task-specific knowledge transfer signals measured during training.

Method: We introduce a gradient-signal-based saliency metric that, at each training step, estimates per-layer semantic drift (cosine distance from pretrained activations on held-out VQA benchmarks). Layers exceeding a drift threshold are softly regularized via EWC-style penalties rather than hard-frozen, while task-specific action-relevant layers are allowed to adapt freely. A lightweight meta-controller trained on task embeddings predicts the per-layer regularization coefficients.

Experiments: We evaluate on LIBERO benchmark suites (LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, LIBERO-Long), Open-X-Embodiment cross-embodiment splits, and a new real-robot generalization suite. Metrics include success rate, VQA retention scores, training wall-clock time, and sample efficiency compared to uniform insulation and full fine-tuning baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Fine-tuning: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Manipulation Tasks
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation during VLA training preserves pretrained VLM semantics, a uniform insulation strategy across all backbone layers may be suboptimal — some layers encode task-relevant visual-semantic features that should adapt to robotic domains, while others encode general language grounding that should be preserved. The right insulation granularity likely varies by task complexity, embodiment, and data scale. Method: We propose Adaptive Layer-wise Insulation (ALI), a method that learns per-layer insulation coefficients via a lightweight meta-gradient signal measuring knowledge retention (via VQA probe accuracy on held-out vision-language benchmarks) versus policy performance improvement. During VLA training, each transformer layer receives a learned gating weight balancing gradient flow from the action expert versus frozen initialization. We further investigate whether insulation needs differ for visual encoder layers versus language model layers versus cross-attention bridges. Experiments: We evaluate on FurnitureBench, LIBERO, and a real-robot dexterous manipulation suite across 50+ tasks. We measure: (1) VQA benchmark degradation as knowledge preservation proxy, (2) task success rate, (3) generalization to novel object categories and language instructions, (4) training convergence speed. We compare against uniform insulation, full fine-tuning, and LoRA baselines, analyzing which layer groups benefit most from adaptive gating.

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Fine-tuning: When and What to Unfreeze for Optimal Knowledge-Action Balance
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation during VLA training treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, but different layers encode different levels of semantic abstraction (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantic concepts vs. spatial reasoning). Naively freezing or unfreezing the entire backbone may be suboptimal—early layers may benefit from task-specific adaptation while later semantic layers should remain insulated. Proposed Method: We introduce Dynamic Layer-wise Insulation Scheduling (DLIS), a principled approach that (1) measures per-layer knowledge degradation during VLA training using probing classifiers on semantic benchmarks at regular intervals, (2) automatically identifies which layers are most vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting, and (3) applies a curriculum-style unfreezing schedule that progressively exposes lower layers to action-relevant gradients while maintaining stronger insulation on semantically-rich upper layers. We combine this with gradient magnitude monitoring to trigger re-insulation when drift exceeds thresholds. Experiments: We evaluate on SimplerEnv and real robot manipulation tasks, measuring (a) task success rates, (b) retained VLM benchmark performance (VQA, captioning), (c) training convergence speed, and (d) out-of-distribution generalization to novel objects/instructions. Ablations compare against full freezing, full fine-tuning, uniform insulation, and the pi.website knowledge insulation baseline across multiple VLM backbone sizes (3B, 7B, 13B parameters).

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description:
Problem: Knowledge Insulation (KI) in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity requiring uniform protection, but different transformer layers encode fundamentally different knowledge (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantics). When adapting a single VLA to diverse robot morphologies (manipulators, mobile robots, quadrupeds), some semantic knowledge may be irrelevant or even harmful, while visual grounding remains universally valuable. A one-size-fits-all insulation strategy may over-protect irrelevant layers or under-protect critical ones.

Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Adaptive Knowledge Insulation (LAKI), which measures per-layer knowledge retention using probing classifiers trained on VLM benchmark tasks (VQA, object recognition) throughout VLA training. Using these signals, we apply a differentiable gating mechanism that dynamically adjusts gradient flow through each layer based on its knowledge-retention score. For cross-morphology generalization, we train a lightweight morphology-conditioned router that learns which layer subsets to insulate per robot type.

Experiments: (1) Compare LAKI vs. uniform KI on OpenVLA and π0 across three robot morphologies using standard benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboSuite, real-world manipulation). (2) Ablate layer-selection strategies. (3) Measure knowledge retention via VLM benchmark probing throughout training. (4) Evaluate zero-shot transfer to unseen morphologies. We hypothesize LAKI achieves better semantic retention with faster policy convergence than uniform insulation.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Fine-Tuning: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation techniques fix a static boundary between the frozen VLM backbone and trainable action modules. However, different robot morphologies (manipulators, quadrupeds, humanoids) and task types (dexterous manipulation, locomotion, navigation) may require varying degrees of semantic knowledge adaptation across VLM layers. A rigid insulation strategy may over-constrain semantically relevant layers for some tasks while under-protecting them for others. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Semantic Insulation (ASI), a technique that automatically identifies which VLM layers contain task-relevant semantic representations (using gradient-based importance scores and representational similarity analysis against frozen reference VLMs) and applies layer-specific insulation strength accordingly. Rather than a binary freeze/unfreeze decision, ASI uses soft LoRA-based gating that dynamically adjusts the update magnitude per layer per task during training. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate across three robot morphologies (Franka arm, Unitree quadruped, Boston Dynamics humanoid) with 5+ task categories; (2) Measure semantic retention via VQA benchmarks at intermediate training checkpoints; (3) Compare against full insulation, no insulation, and uniform LoRA baselines on sample efficiency and generalization to novel objects/environments; (4) Ablate importance scoring methods. Primary metric: combined semantic retention score × task success rate.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Models: When and Where to Insulate During Continual Robot Skill Acquisition
description: Problem: When VLA models acquire new robot skills sequentially (e.g., first learning manipulation, then locomotion, then dexterous grasping), naive continual fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting of both previously learned skills and underlying VLM semantic knowledge. The knowledge insulation technique from the anchor paper provides a static solution during initial training, but continual learning requires dynamic decisions about which layers to protect at each learning stage. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gradient-Sensitivity Insulation (AGSI), which computes per-layer Fisher Information Matrix approximations at each continual learning step to identify which VLM backbone layers are most critical for retaining prior skill knowledge and semantic grounding. AGSI dynamically adjusts insulation strength (via selective gradient blocking and EWC-style penalties) per layer per task, allowing high-plasticity layers to adapt while protecting semantically rich layers. We combine this with a task-conditioned action expert that grows modularly for each new skill domain. Experiments: (1) Sequential acquisition of 5 diverse robot skills on a real robot arm, measuring forward transfer, backward transfer, and semantic probe accuracy; (2) Ablations comparing static insulation vs. AGSI vs. no insulation; (3) Scaling experiments across VLM backbone sizes (3B, 7B, 13B parameters); (4) Evaluation on LIBERO and RoboSuite continual benchmarks.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Vision-Language Backbones
description:
Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs proposes insulating the VLM backbone during action expert training, but applies this uniformly across all layers. Different VLM layers encode qualitatively different information (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantic reasoning), and blanket insulation may unnecessarily sacrifice task-relevant adaptation signals while targeted layer-wise strategies could better preserve semantic knowledge where it matters most.

Proposed Method: We introduce Gradient-Informed Selective Insulation (GISI), which dynamically identifies which VLM layers to freeze or fine-tune during VLA training based on two signals: (1) a layer-wise knowledge retention score measuring cosine similarity of layer activations on held-out VLM benchmarks before and after gradient steps, and (2) a task relevance score measuring gradient magnitude attributed to each layer for robot control loss. GISI uses these scores to construct a per-layer insulation schedule that freezes semantically critical layers early and relaxes constraints on task-relevant layers as training progresses.

Experiments: (1) Systematic ablation comparing uniform insulation, no insulation, and GISI on OpenVLA and pi0-style architectures across 10 manipulation tasks. (2) VLM benchmark retention (VQAv2, MMMU) vs. robot task success tradeoff curves. (3) Analysis of which layers contribute to generalization on novel object/instruction combinations. (4) Training efficiency (wall-clock time to convergence) comparison. Expected outcome: GISI achieves better semantic retention and task generalization than uniform insulation with comparable inference speed.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Models: A Gradient-Based Analysis of Which VLM Layers to Insulate
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLA models treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, but different transformer layers encode qualitatively different knowledge (low-level visual features, mid-level spatial relations, high-level semantic concepts). Naively freezing the entire backbone wastes adaptation capacity, while full fine-tuning degrades semantic knowledge. An open question is: which layers benefit most from insulation, and which should adapt freely for control tasks?

Proposed Method: We propose Gradient-Informed Selective Insulation (GISI), which analyzes gradient flow statistics (magnitude, variance, and alignment with the original VLM's representation manifold) across layers during VLA training. Using these signals, we construct a layer-wise insulation schedule that freezes semantically critical layers while allowing control-relevant adaptation in others. We augment this with a lightweight per-layer knowledge retention loss computed against frozen VLM activations, applied selectively based on layer sensitivity scores.

Experiments: (1) Layer-wise gradient and representation drift analysis on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures during diffusion action expert training. (2) Comparison against full insulation, no insulation, and LoRA baselines on FurnitureBench, LIBERO, and real robot manipulation tasks. (3) Ablations on insulation schedules: static vs. dynamic, uniform vs. gradient-informed. (4) Zero-shot generalization to novel object categories as a semantic knowledge retention proxy.

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Fine-tuning: When and Where to Insulate Across Embodiments
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, applying uniform insulation strategies. However, different layers of a VLM encode qualitatively different knowledge (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantics vs. language grounding), and the optimal insulation strategy likely varies across robot embodiments, task complexities, and action space dimensionalities. A one-size-fits-all insulation approach may over-protect some layers while under-protecting others. Method: We propose Dynamic Selective Insulation (DSI), a method that learns per-layer insulation coefficients via a bi-level optimization framework. An outer loop estimates which VLM layers suffer most from catastrophic forgetting (measured via Fisher Information on held-out VLM benchmarks) during action expert integration, while an inner loop trains the VLA normally. We additionally propose curriculum-based insulation schedules that progressively relax insulation as training proceeds, allowing early semantic preservation followed by later cross-modal adaptation. Experiments: We evaluate DSI across three robot platforms (tabletop manipulation, mobile manipulation, locomotion), comparing against uniform insulation baselines from the anchor paper. Metrics include downstream task success rate, training convergence speed, VLM benchmark retention (VQA, captioning), and cross-embodiment transfer. We ablate insulation granularity (per-layer vs. per-attention-head) and schedule shapes (linear, cosine, step).

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs focuses on preserving VLM semantics during action expert integration, but the optimal insulation strategy likely varies dramatically across robot morphologies (manipulation arms, legged robots, dexterous hands) and task types (contact-rich, long-horizon, bimanual). A single global insulation strategy may over-constrain adaptation for morphologies requiring novel visual grounding while under-protecting semantics for simpler pick-and-place tasks.

Proposed Method: We introduce Morphology-Adaptive Selective Insulation (MASI), which learns per-layer insulation masks conditioned on (1) gradient signal magnitude during action expert training, (2) layer-wise semantic retention scores measured via VLM probing tasks, and (3) morphology-specific action complexity metrics. Rather than uniform backbone freezing, MASI applies differentiable soft gating per transformer layer, allowing middle layers to adapt for morphology-specific visual features while protecting early semantic layers and late reasoning layers.

Experiments: We evaluate on four robot platforms (Franka, Allegro hand, Unitree quadruped, bimanual ALOHA) using both diffusion and flow-matching action experts. Metrics include: task success rate, training convergence speed, VLM knowledge retention (VQA benchmarks), and zero-shot generalization to novel object categories. Ablations compare uniform freezing, gradient-based layer selection, and our adaptive approach across data regimes (10, 100, 1000 demonstrations).

title: Selective Layer Freezing for Multi-Task VLA Generalization: When to Insulate, When to Adapt
description:
Problem: Knowledge Insulation (KI) uniformly protects the VLM backbone during VLA training, but this one-size-fits-all approach may be suboptimal — some VLM layers encode task-transferable semantics that should be preserved, while others benefit from task-specific fine-tuning for precise motor control. The optimal insulation strategy likely varies by layer depth, task diversity, and domain gap between pretraining and deployment.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Selective Insulation (ASI), which learns per-layer insulation coefficients via a lightweight meta-gradient procedure. During VLA training, a small held-out semantic probe set (VQA tasks) provides gradients that determine which layers to insulate. Layers whose gradients from action learning conflict with semantic preservation receive higher insulation coefficients, while layers that can adapt without semantic degradation are allowed to fine-tune freely. This creates a continuous insulation spectrum rather than a binary freeze/unfreeze decision.

Experiments: (1) Compare ASI against uniform KI and full fine-tuning on OpenVLA and π0 across 10+ manipulation tasks in LIBERO and RLBench; (2) Measure semantic retention via VQA benchmarks throughout training; (3) Evaluate few-shot generalization to novel objects and instructions; (4) Ablate meta-gradient frequency and probe set size; (5) Analyze which layers consistently receive high vs. low insulation coefficients across tasks to derive architectural insights.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs focuses on preserving VLM backbone integrity during action expert integration, but assumes a single robot morphology during training. When deploying VLAs across heterogeneous robot platforms (manipulators, quadrupeds, humanoids), different morphologies may require conflicting adaptations to backbone layers, creating tension between morphology-specific control learning and general semantic preservation. Naively applying uniform insulation ignores that different backbone layers may need morphology-specific fine-tuning while others benefit from strict insulation. Method: We propose Morphology-Aware Selective Insulation (MASI), which learns per-layer insulation masks conditioned on robot morphology embeddings. Using a lightweight meta-learning approach, MASI identifies which VLM layers are semantically critical (always insulated), which are morphology-agnostic control-relevant (shared fine-tuning), and which are morphology-specific (selective unfreezing). We introduce a gradient-based layer importance score that dynamically adjusts insulation strength during multi-robot co-training. Experiments: We train on three robot morphologies simultaneously (Franka arm, ANYmal quadruped, Unitree H1 humanoid) using simulation and real hardware, measuring (1) cross-morphology generalization on novel tasks, (2) VLM semantic retention via vision-language benchmarks throughout training, (3) training convergence speed versus full insulation/no insulation baselines, and (4) zero-shot transfer to unseen robot embodiments.

title: Selective Knowledge Insulation via Layer-wise Relevance Probing for Multi-Task VLA Generalization
description:
Problem: While knowledge insulation preserves VLM semantics during VLA training, uniform insulation treats all VLM layers equally, potentially over-constraining action-relevant layers or under-protecting semantically rich ones. Different layers encode different abstraction levels (low-level textures vs. high-level concepts), and a one-size-fits-all insulation strategy may leave performance on the table for multi-task generalization.

Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-wise Relevance-Guided Insulation (LRGI), which dynamically determines per-layer insulation strength based on each layer's semantic knowledge retention score. We first probe frozen VLM layers using lightweight linear classifiers on vision-language benchmark tasks (VQA, object grounding) to quantify semantic content per layer. We then parameterize insulation strength as a differentiable per-layer gate, trained jointly with the action expert via a dual-objective loss: task performance plus a semantic preservation regularizer computed from layer-wise probing scores. Layers with high semantic content receive stronger insulation; action-interface layers receive weaker insulation to allow task-specific adaptation.

Experiments: We evaluate on LIBERO multi-task benchmarks and FurnitureBench across 50+ manipulation tasks, comparing uniform insulation, no insulation, and LRGI. Metrics include task success rate, training convergence speed, semantic benchmark degradation (VQA accuracy post-training), and zero-shot generalization to novel object categories and instructions.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation technique proposed for VLAs assumes a monolithic strategy—insulating the VLM backbone uniformly during action expert training. However, different robot morphologies (manipulators, quadrupeds, humanoids) and task types (semantic reasoning-heavy vs. motor-skill-heavy) likely require different degrees of backbone insulation at different layers, and a one-size-fits-all approach may leave performance on the table. Proposed Method: We introduce Morphology-Adaptive Selective Insulation (MASI), which learns per-layer insulation gates via a lightweight meta-gradient procedure. During VLA finetuning, we jointly optimize task performance and a knowledge retention objective (measuring VLM benchmark scores on held-out captioning/VQA tasks) to automatically discover which layers benefit from insulation vs. adaptation. Gates are parameterized as continuous interpolations between frozen and trainable states, annealed during training. This avoids manual design choices about which layers to freeze. Planned Experiments: (1) Compare MASI against uniform insulation and no-insulation baselines across three robot platforms (Franka arm, Unitree quadruped, Agility Cassie) on 20+ tasks in simulation and real world; (2) Measure VLM knowledge retention via standard benchmarks at each training checkpoint; (3) Ablate gate parameterization, annealing schedules, and the retention objective weight; (4) Analyze which layers are gated open vs. closed across morphologies to provide interpretability insights about VLM-to-VLA knowledge transfer.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for Continual VLA Adaptation: Preserving Semantic Knowledge During Task-Specific Fine-Tuning
description: Problem: When deployed VLA models need to adapt to new tasks or environments through continued fine-tuning, they face catastrophic forgetting of both semantic VLM knowledge and previously learned manipulation skills. While knowledge insulation addresses the initial VLM-to-VLA training transition, the problem of continual adaptation remains unaddressed. Method: We propose Semantic-Anchor Continual Adaptation (SACA), which dynamically identifies and selectively freezes VLM backbone layers whose representations are most critical for semantic grounding during task-specific fine-tuning. We use a lightweight Fisher information-based importance scoring computed on a small held-out semantic evaluation set to rank layers, then apply graduated freezing—fully freezing top-k semantically critical layers, applying LoRA adapters to intermediate layers, and allowing full updates only to action-expert modules. We additionally introduce a semantic consistency regularization loss that penalizes drift in intermediate representations of the frozen backbone. Experiments: We evaluate on a continual manipulation benchmark spanning 10 sequential task families in simulation (RLBench) and 5 real-robot task sequences, measuring (1) backward transfer on previously learned tasks, (2) semantic grounding retention via VQA probes, (3) forward transfer to held-out tasks, and (4) wall-clock adaptation time. Ablations compare Fisher importance vs. gradient-based vs. uniform freezing strategies.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When Does Backbone Knowledge Matter for Manipulation?
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation preserves VLM semantic understanding during VLA training, it treats the backbone as a monolithic unit. Different VLM layers encode qualitatively different knowledge (low-level visual features, mid-level object semantics, high-level language grounding), yet their individual contributions to downstream manipulation success and their vulnerability to corruption during action expert training remain unstudied. A principled layer-wise freezing strategy could offer better trade-offs than full insulation. Proposed Method: We introduce a gradient-sensitivity analysis framework that measures, for each transformer layer, (1) the gradient interference from action expert training and (2) the layer's contribution to task-relevant semantic representations via probing classifiers on manipulation-relevant concepts (object identity, spatial relations, affordances). Using these two signals jointly, we derive a task-adaptive selective freezing schedule that freezes only high-interference, high-semantic-value layers while allowing low-sensitivity layers to fine-tune for embodied adaptation. We additionally propose a lightweight KL-divergence regularizer applied selectively to vulnerable layers as a soft alternative to hard freezing. Experiments: We evaluate on LIBERO, Calvin, and a real robot benchmark across 3 VLM backbones (PaliGemma, InternVL, Qwen-VL), measuring generalization to novel object categories, training convergence speed, and layer-wise semantic retention via probing. We compare against full fine-tuning, full insulation, and LoRA baselines, demonstrating that selective freezing achieves better generalization-efficiency Pareto fronts.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Adaptation: Preserving Semantic Knowledge During Domain Shifts
description: Problem: When deployed VLA models need to adapt to new robot morphologies, environments, or task distributions, continual fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting of both VLM semantic knowledge and previously learned manipulation skills—a compound forgetting problem not addressed by knowledge insulation during initial training. Proposed Method: We propose Dynamic Semantic Anchoring (DSA), a continual adaptation framework that identifies which VLM backbone layers contain task-transferable semantic knowledge versus morphology-specific control representations using Fisher Information Matrix estimates computed on a small semantic probe dataset. DSA selectively freezes high-semantic-value layers during domain adaptation, while allowing control-relevant layers and action experts to adapt freely. Additionally, we introduce an elastic weight consolidation variant specifically calibrated for VLA architectures that applies differential regularization strength based on each layer's measured semantic vs. control contribution ratio. Experiments: We evaluate on three continual adaptation scenarios: (1) adapting a tabletop manipulation VLA to a mobile manipulation robot, (2) sequential adaptation across five object categories with increasing visual diversity, and (3) sim-to-real transfer. We measure semantic retention via VQA probing benchmarks throughout adaptation, final task success rates, and sample efficiency. Baselines include naive fine-tuning, LoRA adaptation, and the knowledge insulation method from the anchor paper applied at adaptation time. We hypothesize DSA achieves 25-40% better semantic retention with comparable task performance.

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Fine-Tuning: When and What to Insulate Across Training Stages
description:
Problem: The knowledge insulation paper establishes that protecting the VLM backbone during VLA training improves both convergence speed and semantic knowledge retention. However, it treats insulation as a static binary choice—either the backbone is protected or it is not. In practice, different layers encode different levels of semantic abstraction, and optimal insulation strategies likely vary across training stages (early exploration vs. late refinement) and task types (semantic grounding vs. low-level motor control).

Proposed Method: We propose dynamic, layer-wise insulation scheduling (DLIS), where insulation strength per transformer layer is treated as a learnable or heuristic-driven schedule over training time. We implement three variants: (1) gradient-magnitude-based scheduling that selectively unfreezes layers when their gradients stabilize, (2) representation drift monitoring using CKA similarity to the original VLM to trigger adaptive freezing, and (3) task-conditioned insulation where semantic-heavy tasks maintain stricter backbone protection than motor-primitive tasks.

Experiments: We evaluate on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures across three benchmarks: LIBERO, Calvin, and real-robot manipulation tasks. Metrics include training wall-clock time, downstream language grounding accuracy (VQA probes on frozen representations), and task success rates under distribution shift. We compare against static insulation baselines from the anchor paper, standard fine-tuning, and LoRA-based approaches, ablating schedule types and granularity.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Tasks
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation technique treats VLM backbone preservation as a binary or uniform choice during VLA training. However, different robot tasks stress different semantic knowledge layers—manipulation tasks rely heavily on spatial/object representations in mid-to-late vision layers, while instruction-following relies on language semantic layers. Uniform insulation may over-constrain task-relevant layers while under-protecting irrelevant ones, leaving performance on the table. Proposed Method: We introduce Task-Adaptive Selective Insulation (TASI), which dynamically identifies which VLM backbone layers to insulate versus fine-tune based on layer-wise relevance propagation scores computed on a small task-specific validation set before training. We augment this with a gradient-magnitude monitoring scheme that detects when specific layers begin disrupting pretrained representations during action expert integration, triggering targeted insulation mid-training. Planned Experiments: (1) Benchmark TASI against uniform insulation and full fine-tuning across 5 task categories (pick-and-place, articulated object manipulation, long-horizon instruction following, novel object generalization, cross-embodiment transfer) using the OpenVLA and pi0 frameworks. (2) Measure semantic retention via VQA probing at each layer throughout training. (3) Ablate the relevance threshold and timing of insulation triggers. (4) Evaluate sim-to-real transfer on a real robot arm across 20 tasks. Expected outcome: TASI achieves 15-25% better task success while maintaining higher semantic retention than uniform insulation.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Fine-tuning: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Tasks
description: Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs demonstrates that protecting VLM backbone knowledge during action expert training is critical, but treats insulation as a binary, uniform decision across all layers and tasks. Different robot manipulation tasks (e.g., semantic reasoning-heavy tasks like 'pick the ripe fruit' vs. purely geometric tasks like 'insert peg') likely require different degrees of VLM knowledge preservation at different network depths. A one-size-fits-all insulation strategy may over-constrain adaptation for geometry-heavy tasks or under-protect semantics for language-grounded tasks. Proposed Method: We introduce Task-Adaptive Selective Insulation (TASI), a method that learns per-layer, per-task insulation coefficients via a small meta-learning phase. Using Fisher Information to estimate which layers encode task-relevant vs. generic semantic knowledge, TASI dynamically gates gradient flow through backbone layers during VLA fine-tuning. A lightweight task-type classifier routes incoming tasks to pre-computed insulation masks, enabling efficient multi-task training. Planned Experiments: (1) Ablation of insulation depth profiles on LIBERO benchmark suite across semantic vs. geometric task splits; (2) Comparison against uniform insulation baseline from anchor paper on RT-2 and OpenVLA architectures; (3) Evaluation of knowledge retention via VQA probes post-training; (4) Real-robot experiments on a Franka arm with 10 diverse tasks measuring both success rate and inference latency.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Knowledge Preservation: A Gradient-Based Analysis of Which VLM Layers Matter for Generalization
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation techniques for VLA models (e.g., gradient blocking between action experts and VLM backbone) treat the backbone monolithically, but different transformer layers in pretrained VLMs likely contribute differently to semantic generalization versus low-level motor control adaptation. Naively insulating all layers may over-constrain useful fine-tuning, while insufficient insulation degrades semantic knowledge.

Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Selective Knowledge Preservation (LSKP), which uses Fisher Information Matrix estimates computed on diverse vision-language tasks to identify and rank VLM layers by their semantic knowledge density. During VLA training, we apply a graduated insulation schedule: high-knowledge layers receive stronger gradient isolation from the action expert, while lower layers are allowed greater adaptation. We combine this with a lightweight semantic probe evaluated continuously during training to detect knowledge degradation and trigger dynamic re-insulation.

Experiments: (1) Compute Fisher-based layer importance profiles across VLMs of varying scales (7B-70B). (2) Compare LSKP against full insulation, no insulation, and LoRA-based approaches on LIBERO, RLBench, and real robot manipulation benchmarks measuring both task success and semantic generalization (novel object/instruction transfer). (3) Ablate graduation schedules and probe sensitivity. (4) Analyze training speed vs. generalization tradeoffs across regimes.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge During Task Expansion
description:
Problem: Vision-Language-Action models trained on one robot task distribution suffer catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuned on new tasks. While knowledge insulation addresses degradation during initial VLA training, continual deployment requires sequentially adding new skills without erasing previously acquired semantic or motor knowledge. Existing continual learning methods (EWC, PackNet) were designed for classification, not continuous control with hybrid discrete-continuous architectures.

Proposed Method: We introduce Semantic-Motor Decoupled Continual Learning (SMDCL), which separately manages plasticity in the VLM backbone versus the action expert during sequential task acquisition. Building on the insulation insight, we compute per-layer Fisher information separately for semantic (language-image alignment) and motor (action prediction) objectives, then apply task-specific soft masks that allow the action expert to adapt freely while constraining backbone layers proportional to their semantic importance scores. A lightweight episodic replay buffer stores compact VLM-embedding summaries rather than raw observations, reducing memory overhead.

Experiments: (1) Sequential training on 8 manipulation tasks in simulation (RLBench), measuring forward transfer and backward interference. (2) Real robot experiments on a 6-DOF arm learning 5 skills sequentially. (3) Ablations comparing full fine-tuning, standard EWC, backbone freezing, and SMDCL on both task success rates and VLM benchmark retention (VQAv2, GQA). (4) Scaling analysis across VLM backbone sizes (3B, 7B, 13B parameters).

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Catastrophic Forgetting: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Manipulation Tasks
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation techniques prevent VLM backbone degradation during VLA training, a fixed insulation strategy may be suboptimal across diverse manipulation domains. Some tasks (e.g., novel object grasping) heavily rely on preserved semantic knowledge, while others (e.g., force-controlled assembly) may benefit from deeper backbone adaptation. A static insulation scheme cannot capture this spectrum, potentially leaving performance gains unrealized. Method: We propose Task-Adaptive Knowledge Insulation (TAKI), which dynamically determines per-layer insulation strength based on task semantic complexity. Specifically, we compute a 'semantic reliance score' for each task using probing classifiers that measure how much VLM intermediate representations contribute to task success. Layers with high semantic reliance scores receive stronger gradient insulation (via scaled stop-gradients or LoRA rank reduction), while task-specific layers adapt more freely. We further introduce a curriculum that gradually relaxes insulation as task-specific representations stabilize during training. Experiments: We evaluate on BridgeV2, OXE, and a new benchmark spanning 5 manipulation categories with varying semantic complexity. Metrics include final success rate, training convergence speed, retained VLM semantic accuracy (via VQA probing), and cross-task transfer. We ablate insulation schedules, layer selection strategies, and compare against fixed insulation baselines from the anchor paper.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation during VLA training preserves VLM semantics, the optimal insulation strategy likely varies across robot morphologies (manipulators, legged robots, dexterous hands) and task domains (contact-rich manipulation, navigation, whole-body control). A single fixed insulation scheme may over-constrain adaptation for some morphologies while under-protecting knowledge for others. Proposed Method: We introduce morphology-aware adaptive insulation, which dynamically determines which VLM layers to freeze/insulate based on (1) task-specific probing classifiers that measure semantic knowledge retention per layer during early training, and (2) gradient conflict analysis between the VLM backbone and action expert that identifies layers where action learning most disrupts visual-semantic representations. We develop a lightweight 'insulation scheduler' that progressively releases frozen layers as action expert competence (measured via validation loss) stabilizes, enabling fine-grained semantic adaptation where beneficial while protecting critical representations. Experiments: We evaluate on five robot platforms across 50+ tasks in simulation (IsaacLab, ManiSkill3) and two real-robot setups, comparing fixed insulation, no insulation, and our adaptive method on task success rate, training convergence speed, and semantic probing accuracy on held-out VQA benchmarks. Ablations examine scheduler timing, layer selection criteria, and transfer to novel objects/instructions.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge Across Sequential Task Acquisition
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation addresses VLM degradation during initial VLA training, robots in deployment must continually acquire new manipulation skills without catastrophically forgetting previously learned ones or the underlying semantic knowledge from VLM pretraining. Current VLA fine-tuning strategies lack principled methods for sequential skill acquisition that maintain both task performance and semantic grounding. Proposed Method: We introduce Semantic-Preserving Continual VLA (SP-CVLA), which combines insights from knowledge insulation with elastic weight consolidation tailored for VLA architectures. We identify 'semantic anchor layers' — VLM backbone layers most critical for semantic knowledge retention using Fisher information computed over a vision-language probing dataset — and apply layer-specific learning rate schedules and EWC penalties during sequential task fine-tuning. The action expert receives unrestricted updates while semantic anchor layers are heavily regularized, and a lightweight task-specific adapter is inserted per new skill. Experiments: We evaluate on a benchmark of 10 sequentially introduced manipulation tasks in simulation (IsaacLab) and 5 real-robot tasks, measuring: (1) forward transfer to new tasks, (2) backward transfer / catastrophic forgetting on previous tasks, (3) VLM semantic probing accuracy throughout training, and (4) zero-shot generalization to novel objects using CLIP-based semantic similarity. Baselines include EWC, PackNet, LoRA fine-tuning, and naive sequential fine-tuning.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Models: When and What to Insulate During Continual Robot Skill Acquisition
description: Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs demonstrates that protecting VLM backbone knowledge during initial VLA training is critical. However, robots must continually acquire new skills after deployment without catastrophic forgetting of both semantic VLM knowledge and previously learned motor skills. The optimal insulation strategy for continual learning remains unexplored—static full-backbone freezing may prevent necessary adaptation while full fine-tuning causes forgetting. Proposed Method: We introduce Dynamic Selective Insulation (DSI), a continual learning framework that automatically identifies which VLM layers require insulation at each new skill acquisition phase. DSI uses gradient sensitivity analysis and Fisher Information to score each transformer layer's contribution to (1) semantic knowledge retention and (2) existing motor skill performance, then applies layer-specific learning rate scaling and optional LoRA adapters to layers needing plasticity. A small episodic memory buffer stores representative observations from prior tasks to enable online insulation boundary recalibration.
