Planned Experiments: We evaluate on a simulated kitchen manipulation benchmark with 20 sequential tasks using a π0-style VLA backbone. Metrics include: forward transfer to new skills, backward transfer (forgetting) of semantic VQA benchmarks, inference latency, and sample efficiency per new skill. Ablations compare static full-freeze, no-freeze, full DSI, and Fisher-only variants, demonstrating that adaptive insulation outperforms fixed strategies across the continual learning sequence.

title: Modality-Selective Freezing: Preserving Visual and Linguistic Knowledge Independently During VLA Fine-tuning
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic unit, applying uniform protection strategies. However, visual encoders and language modules within VLMs may degrade at different rates and for different reasons when action experts are introduced. Selectively understanding and preserving each modality's knowledge could yield better generalization and faster adaptation than holistic insulation.

Method: We propose Modality-Selective Freezing (MSF), a training protocol that independently monitors and regulates knowledge drift in the visual and linguistic pathways of the VLM backbone during VLA fine-tuning. We introduce per-modality 'knowledge retention scores' computed via lightweight probing tasks (object recognition for vision, instruction following for language) evaluated periodically during training. Based on these scores, MSF dynamically adjusts layer-wise learning rate scaling and LoRA rank allocation separately for visual and linguistic components, allowing the more degraded modality to recover while the stable one continues adapting.

Experiments: We evaluate on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures across three benchmarks: LIBERO, RLBench, and a real-robot manipulation suite. Ablations compare uniform insulation, vision-only freezing, language-only freezing, and MSF. Metrics include task success rate, VQA retention scores, zero-shot generalization to novel instructions, and training convergence speed. We hypothesize MSF outperforms uniform insulation particularly on language-conditioned generalization tasks.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for Continual VLA Adaptation: Preserving Semantic Knowledge During Task-Specific Fine-Tuning
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation during initial VLA training is addressed by the anchor paper, but a complementary challenge remains: when a deployed VLA must continually adapt to new tasks or environments (e.g., new object categories, novel manipulation primitives), repeated fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting of both VLM semantic knowledge and previously learned motor skills. Existing continual learning methods ignore the heterogeneous knowledge structure of VLA models (semantic vs. motor vs. visuomotor binding). Proposed Method: We introduce Structured Elastic Weight Consolidation for VLAs (SEWC-VLA), which computes separate Fisher information matrices for three knowledge types: (1) VLM semantic layers, (2) visuomotor binding layers identified via cross-attention activation analysis, and (3) action expert parameters. During continual fine-tuning, layer-type-specific consolidation strengths are applied, allowing action experts to adapt freely while strongly protecting semantic representations. We additionally propose a lightweight 'knowledge probe' evaluated periodically during training to trigger adaptive consolidation strength adjustment. Experiments: We evaluate on a continual robotic manipulation benchmark spanning 10 sequential task additions using both simulated (RLBench) and real robot setups, measuring per-task success rate retention, semantic VQA probe accuracy preservation, and adaptation speed. Baselines include EWC, PackNet, LoRA fine-tuning, and the anchor paper's insulation technique applied naively to continual settings.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge Across Sequential Robot Task Acquisition
description: Problem: When VLA models are sequentially fine-tuned on new robot tasks (e.g., moving from tabletop manipulation to mobile manipulation), catastrophic forgetting degrades both previously learned motor skills and the underlying VLM semantic knowledge. Existing knowledge insulation techniques focus on initial VLA training but do not address the continual learning regime where robots must incrementally acquire new capabilities without full retraining. Method: We propose Semantic-Motor Decoupled Continual Learning (SMDCL), which builds on knowledge insulation principles by maintaining separate elastic weight consolidation (EWC) penalties for VLM backbone layers versus action expert layers. Crucially, we compute Fisher information matrices separately for semantic tasks (VQA benchmarks) and motor tasks (trajectory prediction), applying stronger regularization to high-overlap layers identified through gradient similarity analysis. A lightweight task-conditioned gating mechanism selectively activates subsets of action expert parameters per task, minimizing interference. Experiments: We construct a benchmark of five sequential manipulation tasks in simulation (RLBench) and two real-robot tasks, evaluating (1) forward transfer to new tasks, (2) backward transfer/forgetting of old tasks, (3) VLM semantic knowledge retention via VQA probing after each sequential stage, and (4) wall-clock training efficiency. Baselines include naive fine-tuning, EWC, PackNet, and LoRA-based continual learning, demonstrating that SMDCL best preserves the semantic-motor knowledge balance across task sequences.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Manipulation Domains
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation technique proposed for VLAs applies a uniform backbone protection strategy, but different robotic manipulation domains (dexterous hand manipulation, mobile manipulation, contact-rich assembly) likely require different trade-offs between preserving VLM semantic knowledge and adapting lower-level visual features. A one-size-fits-all insulation approach may over-constrain adaptation for visually novel domains while under-protecting semantics for language-heavy tasks. Proposed Method: We propose Domain-Adaptive Layer Insulation (DALI), a method that automatically determines per-layer insulation strength by computing task-specific Fisher information scores on a small held-out task dataset before VLA fine-tuning begins. Layers with high Fisher information relative to the new task receive reduced insulation (allowed to adapt), while layers critical to semantic VLM knowledge retain strong insulation. We combine this with a lightweight adapter mechanism (LoRA-style) inserted at selectively unfrozen layers to prevent catastrophic forgetting while still enabling task-specific feature learning. Experiments: We evaluate DALI across four manipulation benchmarks spanning language-conditioned tabletop manipulation (LIBERO), dexterous hand tasks (DexArt), mobile manipulation (HelloRobot), and contact-rich assembly (FurnitureBench). We measure semantic knowledge retention via VQA probing, sample efficiency, and cross-task generalization, comparing against uniform insulation, full fine-tuning, and standard LoRA baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Fine-tuning: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Tasks
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone uniformly, applying the same insulation strategy regardless of task semantics or robot morphology. However, different downstream tasks (e.g., language-conditioned grasping vs. long-horizon manipulation) may benefit from different degrees of backbone plasticity at different layers — over-insulation may prevent necessary task-specific adaptation while under-insulation degrades semantic knowledge.

Proposed Method: We introduce Task-Adaptive Layer Insulation (TALI), a method that automatically determines per-layer insulation schedules based on gradient signal analysis during early training. Specifically, we compute layer-wise Fisher information approximations on a small held-out task set to identify which VLM layers carry task-relevant versus generic semantic knowledge. Layers with high task-relevance scores receive dynamic insulation (gradually relaxed over training), while generic layers remain fully insulated. We combine this with a cross-task knowledge distillation loss that penalizes backbone drift on a frozen reference VLM.

Experiments: (1) Compare TALI against uniform insulation on a diverse benchmark spanning 5 robot platforms and 3 task categories using π0-style VLA architecture; (2) Measure VQA retention scores throughout training as a proxy for semantic knowledge preservation; (3) Ablate Fisher threshold hyperparameters and distillation loss weight; (4) Evaluate sample efficiency (tasks learned per GPU-hour) vs. final task success rate tradeoff curves.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Models: A Principled Study of Which VLM Layers to Insulate During Action Expert Training
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic unit to protect, but not all VLM layers contribute equally to semantic knowledge vs. low-level visual processing. Naively freezing all backbone parameters may prevent beneficial adaptation, while unfreezing all layers risks catastrophic forgetting. We need a principled method for selectively insulating only the layers most critical for semantic knowledge transfer.

Proposed Method: We introduce 'gradient-informed selective insulation' (GISI), which identifies semantically critical VLM layers by computing Fisher information scores on a held-out vision-language benchmark before VLA training begins. Layers with high Fisher scores are frozen (insulated) while lower-scoring layers are allowed to adapt with reduced learning rates. We further propose a dynamic threshold that gradually unfreezes high-Fisher layers as training stabilizes, allowing late-stage fine-tuning without catastrophic forgetting.

Experiments: (1) Evaluate GISI against full-freeze, full-finetune, and uniform LoRA baselines on LIBERO and OpenX robot manipulation benchmarks measuring both task success rate and VQA retention. (2) Ablate Fisher threshold selection strategies. (3) Profile inference latency to confirm action expert efficiency is preserved. (4) Test out-of-distribution generalization to novel object categories to measure semantic knowledge retention.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and What to Insulate Across Robot Morphologies
description:
Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs demonstrates that protecting VLM backbone knowledge during action expert training improves generalization, but treats insulation as a binary global decision. Different VLM layers encode different semantic abstractions (low-level features vs. high-level reasoning), and the optimal insulation strategy likely varies across robot morphologies (manipulators vs. mobile robots vs. dexterous hands) and task complexity. A uniform insulation policy may over-constrain adaptation for morphologies requiring substantial visuomotor recalibration or under-protect semantic knowledge for semantically rich manipulation tasks.

Method: We propose Morphology-Adaptive Selective Insulation (MASI), which learns a per-layer insulation coefficient jointly with VLA training. Each transformer layer receives a learnable gating parameter controlling gradient flow from the action expert back into the VLM. We initialize gates using a Fisher information-based importance score measuring each layer's contribution to the pretrained VLM's semantic tasks. Gates are regularized toward full insulation, with strength tuned per robot morphology via a small held-out semantic benchmark.

Experiments: (1) Compare MASI against global insulation and no-insulation baselines on three robot platforms (Franka arm, quadruped locomotion, bi-manual manipulation) across 50+ tasks in simulation and real-world; (2) Analyze learned gate patterns across morphologies; (3) Measure semantic knowledge retention via VQA probes at each layer; (4) Evaluate sample efficiency and sim-to-real transfer gaps.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation technique proposed for VLAs applies a uniform insulation strategy across all VLM backbone layers. However, different layers encode different semantic abstractions (low-level visual features vs. high-level language grounding), and different robot morphologies (manipulators vs. quadrupeds vs. dexterous hands) may require preserving different subsets of this knowledge. A one-size-fits-all insulation scheme may over-constrain adaptation for some morphologies while under-protecting semantics for others. Proposed Method: We introduce morphology-aware selective layer insulation (MSLI), which learns a per-layer binary insulation mask jointly during VLA fine-tuning using a differentiable gating mechanism. Each gate is conditioned on robot morphology embeddings and task complexity signals, allowing the model to discover which layers should remain frozen versus adapted for each deployment context. We additionally propose a knowledge retention metric based on probing classifiers at each layer to quantify semantic degradation throughout training. Experiments: We evaluate MSLI on three robot platforms (Franka arm, Unitree quadruped, Allegro hand) across 50+ tasks in simulation (RLBench, Isaac Lab) and real-world settings. Baselines include full fine-tuning, uniform insulation from the anchor paper, and LoRA adaptation. Metrics include task success rate, training convergence speed, and layer-wise semantic retention scores.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Fine-tuning: When to Insulate, When to Adapt
description:
Problem: The knowledge insulation paper treats VLM backbone protection as a binary choice—either freeze or update the backbone during VLA training. However, different layers of a VLM encode qualitatively different knowledge (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantic reasoning), and robot manipulation tasks may benefit from selectively adapting certain layers while preserving others. A static insulation strategy may over-constrain task-relevant adaptation or under-protect semantically critical layers.

Proposed Method: We develop a dynamic, layer-wise insulation scheduling framework that assigns per-layer 'insulation coefficients' based on (1) gradient sensitivity analysis measuring how much each layer's representations shift during action expert training, (2) semantic retention probes measuring task-irrelevant VLM capabilities (VQA, captioning) throughout fine-tuning, and (3) task performance on held-out manipulation benchmarks. We use these signals to learn a lightweight meta-policy that schedules which layers to freeze, LoRA-adapt, or fully fine-tune at each training phase, optimizing a joint objective balancing semantic retention and control performance.

Experiments: We evaluate on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures across LIBERO, RLBench, and real robot tasks. Ablations compare static full-freeze, static full-adaptation, uniform LoRA, and our dynamic scheduling. Metrics include training convergence speed, semantic retention (VQA benchmarks), and manipulation success rates across task distributions, including zero-shot generalization to novel objects and instructions.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When to Insulate, When to Fine-Tune
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone monolithically—either freezing it entirely or allowing full gradient flow. However, different transformer layers encode qualitatively different information (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantic concepts), and blanket insulation may unnecessarily sacrifice task-relevant adaptation while still harming semantic knowledge. Proposed Method: We propose Gradient-Informed Selective Insulation (GISI), which dynamically identifies which VLM layers should remain frozen versus fine-tuned during VLA training. GISI uses a Fisher Information Matrix approximation computed on a small held-out VLM benchmark (e.g., VQA tasks) to score each layer's semantic knowledge density, then applies layer-wise insulation thresholds that preserve high-scoring layers while allowing controlled gradient flow in lower-scoring ones. We further introduce a knowledge retention regularizer applied only to the partially-thawed layers, penalizing drift from the pretrained VLM representations. Planned Experiments: (1) Compare GISI against full insulation and no insulation baselines using π0/OpenVLA-style architectures on LIBERO, MetaWorld, and real robot manipulation benchmarks; (2) Measure VLM capability retention via zero-shot VQA, image captioning, and spatial reasoning benchmarks throughout training; (3) Ablate Fisher threshold sensitivity and regularizer weight; (4) Analyze training convergence speed and final policy success rates across seen/unseen task generalizations.

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Fine-tuning: When and Where to Insulate Matters
description: Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs establishes that protecting the VLM backbone improves training dynamics and knowledge transfer, but treats insulation as a static, uniform design choice applied throughout training. We hypothesize that optimal insulation is neither uniform across layers nor constant across training phases — early layers encoding low-level visual features may need different treatment than semantic reasoning layers, and insulation needs may shift as the action expert matures. Method: We propose Adaptive Curriculum Insulation (ACI), a framework that dynamically schedules which VLM layers receive gradient flow from the action expert based on (1) layer-wise gradient interference metrics computed online, (2) action expert training loss trajectories indicating maturity, and (3) task semantic complexity signals. ACI uses a differentiable gating mechanism that progressively unfreezes layers from top (semantic) to bottom (perceptual) as training stabilizes. Experiments: We evaluate on the LIBERO benchmark suite and real robot manipulation tasks, comparing static insulation, no insulation, and ACI across metrics including: final task success rate, training convergence speed, VLM semantic probing accuracy (VQA retention), and out-of-distribution generalization to novel object appearances and instructions. We ablate gating schedules, layer ordering strategies, and expert maturity thresholds to provide principled guidelines for practitioners deploying VLA systems.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Matters
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation technique from the anchor paper treats VLM backbone protection as a binary choice, but different layers encode different types of knowledge (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantic reasoning) that may benefit from varying degrees of plasticity during VLA fine-tuning. A uniform insulation strategy may over-constrain layers that should adapt (e.g., visual feature layers for novel robot embodiments) while under-protecting semantically critical layers. Method: We propose LayerSense-VLA, a data-driven approach to identify per-layer insulation schedules. We measure task-relevant knowledge retention using a suite of VLM probing tasks (VQA, spatial reasoning, object affordance) after fine-tuning individual layer groups. Based on a layer sensitivity map, we apply graduated insulation: full insulation for top transformer blocks encoding abstract semantics, partial LoRA-style adaptation for mid-level layers, and free adaptation for early visual layers. We also introduce a dynamic schedule that progressively relaxes insulation as training converges. Experiments: We evaluate on Open-X-Embodiment benchmarks and three simulation suites (FurnitureBench, RLBench, MetaWorld) measuring (1) task success rate, (2) knowledge retention via probing accuracy, (3) few-shot generalization to novel objects, and (4) training convergence speed, comparing against full fine-tuning, uniform insulation, and LoRA baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Generalization: When and Where to Insulate During Continual Robot Skill Acquisition
description: Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs addresses catastrophic forgetting during initial VLA training, but real-world robot deployment requires continual learning of new skills without forgetting previously acquired ones or degrading the VLM's semantic grounding. Naively fine-tuning on new tasks (e.g., novel object manipulation, new environments) can corrupt both action-relevant representations and general vision-language knowledge simultaneously. Proposed Method: We propose Adaptive Insulation Scheduling (AIS), a method that dynamically identifies which VLM layers to freeze, partially update, or fully fine-tune during each new skill acquisition phase, guided by (1) gradient conflict scores between new task gradients and a retained VLM semantic probing loss, and (2) task similarity embeddings that estimate how much new skills overlap with existing knowledge. Unlike static insulation, AIS adjusts per-layer update rates across a curriculum of tasks. We further introduce a lightweight semantic drift detector that triggers re-insulation when VLM representations begin diverging from a frozen reference checkpoint. Experiments: We evaluate on a continual manipulation benchmark spanning 10 sequential tasks using a simulated tabletop environment (RLBench) and real robot trials, measuring (1) forward transfer on new tasks, (2) backward transfer on old tasks, (3) VLM semantic probing accuracy across training stages, and (4) wall-clock training efficiency compared to full fine-tuning and static insulation baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs has been studied primarily for a fixed robot morphology and action space. However, real-world deployment requires adapting a single VLA backbone to heterogeneous robot platforms (arms, quadrupeds, dexterous hands) with varying action dimensionalities and control frequencies. Naively applying uniform insulation strategies across morphologies may over-constrain adaptation for high-DoF systems or under-protect semantic knowledge for simpler ones. Method: We propose Morphology-Adaptive Insulation (MAI), a technique that uses layer-wise gradient sensitivity analysis during early training steps to automatically identify which VLM backbone layers are most disrupted by a new action expert's gradients for a given robot morphology. MAI then applies differential insulation schedules—stronger freezing for semantically critical layers, gradual unfreezing for morphology-specific representational layers—guided by a Fisher Information proxy computed per morphology. This yields per-morphology insulation profiles that can be computed cheaply before full training. Experiments: We train a shared π0-style VLA backbone with diffusion action experts across four robot platforms (Franka arm, Unitree quadruped, Allegro hand, mobile manipulator) on simulation benchmarks (Isaac Lab, ManiSkill3) and real-robot tasks. We evaluate task success, VLM semantic retention (VQA probes), training wall-clock time, and cross-morphology transfer, comparing against uniform insulation, no insulation, and full fine-tuning baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and What to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs has been studied primarily for a single robot morphology and action space. However, real-world deployment requires policies that transfer across robot embodiments (arms, quadrupeds, dexterous hands) with vastly different action dimensionalities and control frequencies. It remains unknown whether the optimal insulation strategy—which layers to freeze, for how long, and with what learning rate schedules—is universal or embodiment-specific, and whether forcing a shared insulation policy across morphologies sacrifices task performance or knowledge retention.

Proposed Method: We propose Morphology-Adaptive Insulation (MAI), a meta-learning-inspired approach that learns per-layer insulation scores conditioned on embodiment metadata (DoF count, control frequency, action space statistics). During VLA fine-tuning, a lightweight hypernetwork predicts which VLM backbone layers to protect from gradient corruption introduced by the action expert, dynamically adjusting insulation strength throughout training. We additionally introduce a knowledge retention probe battery—semantic grounding, spatial reasoning, and instruction following benchmarks—applied at regular training checkpoints to quantify knowledge degradation per embodiment.

Experiments: (1) Fine-tune π0-style VLAs on five robot morphologies from OXE dataset; (2) Compare MAI against uniform insulation, no insulation, and full freezing baselines; (3) Measure task success rates, knowledge probe scores, and wall-clock training convergence; (4) Ablate hypernetwork conditioning variables to identify which embodiment features drive insulation decisions.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs focuses on preserving VLM semantics during action expert integration, but current approaches apply uniform insulation strategies across all backbone layers regardless of robot morphology, task complexity, or action space dimensionality. Different robot platforms (manipulators, bipeds, quadrupeds, dexterous hands) may require different layers to remain plastic versus insulated for optimal generalization. Method: We propose Morphology-Adaptive Layer Insulation (MALI), a technique that learns per-layer insulation coefficients jointly with VLA training via a small meta-gradient signal derived from a held-out semantic validation set. MALI maintains a lightweight 'semantic probe' on intermediate VLM layers and dynamically adjusts gradient flow through each transformer block based on semantic degradation signals. This contrasts with the binary/uniform insulation studied in the anchor paper. Experiments: We evaluate MALI across four robot morphologies (Franka arm, Unitree H1, Spot quadruped, Allegro hand) on 100+ tasks in simulation (Isaac Lab, MuJoCo) and 20 real-robot tasks. Metrics include task success rate, semantic knowledge retention (VQA benchmarks), training convergence speed, and cross-morphology transfer. We compare against uniform insulation, no insulation, and LoRA-based adaptation baselines, with ablations on probe design and gradient coefficient granularity.

title: Selective Layer Freezing via Gradient Sensitivity Analysis for Continual VLA Adaptation
description: Problem: When VLA models are deployed on new robot embodiments or task domains after initial training, continual fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting of both motor skills and semantic VLM knowledge. Existing knowledge insulation techniques (e.g., backbone freezing schedules) are applied uniformly, ignoring that different VLM layers contribute heterogeneously to semantic retention versus action generation. Method: We propose SensAdapt, a continual learning framework that dynamically identifies which VLM backbone layers are semantically 'brittle' (high gradient sensitivity to action expert updates) versus 'robust' during each fine-tuning phase. Using Fisher Information Matrix approximations computed cheaply on a small held-out semantic probe dataset (e.g., VQA tasks), we selectively freeze brittle layers while allowing robust layers to adapt. A dual-memory replay buffer interleaves prior task demonstrations with new ones, guided by uncertainty estimates from the flow-matching action head. Experiments: (1) Sequential adaptation across 5 robot embodiments (sim-to-real) measuring forward transfer and backward transfer on both action success rate and VQA semantic benchmarks; (2) Ablations comparing uniform freezing, LoRA-only, and SensAdapt; (3) Analysis of which layer types are consistently brittle across embodiment shifts. We hypothesize SensAdapt retains >85% semantic knowledge while achieving 90% task success on new domains, outperforming uniform insulation baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge Across Sequential Robot Task Acquisition
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation addresses degradation during initial VLA training, robots deployed in the real world must continuously acquire new skills without catastrophic forgetting of previously learned tasks or the underlying VLM semantic knowledge. Current VLA fine-tuning approaches lack principled methods for determining which layers to update when learning new tasks sequentially. Proposed Method: We introduce Semantic Importance-Weighted Continual VLA Training (SIWCT), which combines the knowledge insulation principle with dynamic layer selection for continual learning. Specifically, we compute a 'semantic preservation score' per transformer layer by measuring how much each layer's representations shift during task-specific fine-tuning relative to the pretrained VLM baseline. Layers with high semantic contribution scores are frozen or updated with lower learning rates, while task-specific adapter modules (LoRA) are inserted into less semantically critical layers. A replay buffer of synthetic VLM captioning tasks maintains language grounding. Planned Experiments: (1) Sequential fine-tuning across 10 robot manipulation tasks on a real robot arm and simulated LIBERO benchmark; (2) Ablations comparing full fine-tuning, naive LoRA, knowledge insulation only, and SIWCT; (3) Measuring forward/backward transfer using standardized VLM semantic benchmarks (VQAv2, GQA) after each sequential task; (4) Wall-clock inference time evaluation across methods. Success metric: maintaining >90% VLM semantic benchmark performance while achieving >85% success rate on all sequential tasks.

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Training: When and What to Insulate Across Robot Learning Curricula
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs focuses on static architectural choices (e.g., gradient blocking) applied uniformly throughout training. However, different training phases may benefit from different degrees of VLM backbone plasticity — early curriculum stages may require more semantic adaptation while later fine-tuning stages need stronger insulation to prevent forgetting. No systematic study exists on dynamic, schedule-based insulation strategies for VLA training.

Method: We propose Curriculum-Adaptive Insulation Schedules (CAIS), which dynamically modulate the degree of VLM backbone insulation throughout VLA training. We parameterize insulation as a per-layer gradient scaling coefficient that follows a learned or heuristic schedule, progressing from low insulation (high plasticity) during initial task-agnostic pretraining to high insulation during task-specific fine-tuning. We investigate both rule-based schedules (cosine annealing, step-wise) and meta-learned schedules optimized for downstream generalization.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark CAIS against static full-insulation and no-insulation baselines on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures across diverse manipulation tasks in simulation (LIBERO, RLBench) and real robot settings. (2) Measure semantic knowledge retention via VQA probing throughout training. (3) Ablate schedule shape, per-layer vs. global scheduling, and interaction with diffusion action experts. (4) Evaluate zero-shot generalization to novel object categories as the primary metric.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs has been studied as a global backbone-level strategy, but different layers of a pretrained VLM encode different levels of semantic abstraction. Applying uniform insulation ignores that some layers may benefit from task-specific fine-tuning while others are more susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. Furthermore, it is unclear whether optimal insulation strategies generalize across robot morphologies (manipulators, quadrupeds, humanoids) with different action space dimensionalities and temporal dynamics. Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Adaptive Insulation (LAI), a method that learns per-layer insulation coefficients via a small meta-objective that jointly optimizes task performance and semantic knowledge retention (measured via VLM benchmark probes embedded during training). LAI uses differentiable gating on gradient flow per transformer block, automatically discovering which layers to freeze, partially update, or fully fine-tune. We further condition insulation coefficients on robot morphology embeddings, enabling a single training recipe to generalize across embodiments. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) language-conditioned manipulation (LIBERO, OXE), (2) quadruped locomotion with language commands, and (3) a humanoid whole-body task suite. Baselines include full fine-tuning, uniform insulation from the anchor paper, LoRA, and layer-wise learning rate schedules. We measure training convergence speed, downstream VLM benchmark retention, and zero-shot generalization to novel instructions.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge Across Sequential Task Acquisition
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation addresses VLM degradation during initial VLA training, robots deployed in the real world must continually acquire new manipulation skills without forgetting previously learned tasks or eroding the underlying VLM's semantic representations—a challenge the current insulation framework does not address. Proposed Method: We propose Continual Knowledge-Insulated VLA (CKI-VLA), which combines the backbone insulation technique with a task-specific adapter architecture for continual learning. Specifically, we maintain frozen VLM backbone layers (using the insulation gradients from the anchor work) while training lightweight LoRA-based task adapters for each new skill. We introduce a semantic drift metric—measuring cosine similarity between VLM feature distributions before and after each new task—to monitor knowledge erosion in real-time and trigger selective replay of a small episodic buffer when drift exceeds a threshold. Experiments: (1) Sequential training on 10 RLBench tasks measuring forward transfer, backward transfer, and semantic drift per task; (2) Comparison against naive fine-tuning, EWC, PackNet, and standard knowledge insulation without continual mechanisms; (3) Zero-shot generalization to novel language instructions after 10-task sequences; (4) Ablations on adapter rank, replay buffer size, and drift threshold sensitivity. Success metric: maintaining >90% of single-task performance while limiting semantic drift below baseline VLA training.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When to Insulate, When to Adapt
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone uniformly, but different layers encode different types of knowledge (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantic reasoning). Blanket insulation may over-constrain adaptation for tasks requiring novel semantic grounding, while insufficient insulation degrades pretrained knowledge. We need a principled, task-adaptive approach to determine which VLM layers to insulate versus fine-tune during VLA training.

Proposed Method: We introduce Gradient-Guided Selective Insulation (GGSI), which dynamically identifies layer-wise contribution to both semantic knowledge retention (measured via probing classifiers on held-out VLM benchmarks) and task-specific control performance during early training. Using Fisher Information estimates computed on a small calibration set of robot demonstrations, GGSI assigns per-layer insulation scores and applies a soft gating mechanism that interpolates between frozen and trainable states. This allows task-relevant layers to adapt while protecting semantically critical ones.

Experiments: (1) Compare GGSI against full insulation, no insulation, and fixed top/bottom-k layer freezing baselines on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures. (2) Evaluate on diverse manipulation tasks spanning novel object categories, spatial reasoning, and language-conditioned instructions. (3) Measure VLM benchmark degradation (VQA, POPE) alongside robot success rates. (4) Ablate Fisher Information threshold sensitivity and calibration set size. We expect GGSI to outperform uniform insulation particularly on tasks requiring semantic generalization to out-of-distribution instructions.

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Fine-tuning: When and What to Unfreeze Matters
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs addresses catastrophic forgetting of VLM semantics during action expert training, but treats insulation as a static design choice. In practice, different VLM layers encode different abstraction levels (low-level vision vs. high-level semantics), and optimal insulation likely varies across training phases and task complexity. A rigid freeze/unfreeze strategy may over-constrain adaptation or under-protect critical semantic representations.

Proposed Method: We introduce Dynamic Insulation Scheduling (DIS), a method that progressively and selectively unfreezes VLM backbone layers during VLA training based on gradient signal alignment between action expert losses and VLM layer representations. Specifically, we compute a layer-wise 'semantic drift score' measuring KL divergence between frozen and current layer output distributions on held-out VLM benchmarks. Layers exceeding a drift threshold are re-frozen mid-training. We combine this with a curriculum that initially insulates all backbone layers, then gradually permits fine-tuning of lower-level visual layers while permanently insulating higher semantic layers.

Experiments: (1) Compare DIS against static insulation and no-insulation baselines on OpenVLA/π0 benchmarks across manipulation tasks. (2) Evaluate semantic retention via VQA and captioning benchmarks throughout training. (3) Test generalization to novel objects and language instructions. (4) Ablate drift threshold sensitivity and unfreezing curriculum schedules. (5) Measure wall-clock training efficiency and final policy success rates on real robot hardware.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for Continual VLA Adaptation: Preserving Semantic Knowledge During Task-Specific Fine-Tuning
description: Problem: When VLA models trained on broad manipulation datasets are fine-tuned for specific deployment environments or novel task distributions, catastrophic forgetting of both semantic VLM knowledge and previously learned motor skills is a critical bottleneck. Current knowledge insulation techniques focus on initial VLA training but do not address continual adaptation scenarios where a deployed robot must specialize to new tasks without losing generalization. Proposed Method: We introduce Gradient-Gated Continual Adaptation (GGCA), a method that dynamically identifies which VLM backbone layers are most semantically sensitive during task-specific fine-tuning using Fisher Information Matrix estimates computed on a small held-out semantic probe dataset. Layers exceeding a sensitivity threshold receive scaled-down gradient updates via learnable gating coefficients, while the action expert and lower-level visual features adapt freely. We additionally propose a semantic drift regularization loss that penalizes deviation of intermediate VLM representations from their pre-adaptation distributions. Experiments: We evaluate on a robot manipulation benchmark requiring sequential specialization across 5 task domains (tool use, deformable objects, articulated furniture, liquid handling, outdoor navigation) using a π0-style VLA backbone. We measure (1) task-specific performance after adaptation, (2) zero-shot generalization on held-out semantic tasks, (3) training efficiency, and compare against EWC, LoRA-only fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning baselines. Ablations isolate contributions of Fisher gating versus semantic drift regularization.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Knowledge Preservation: A Layer-wise Relevance Analysis Approach
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation paper shows that naively coupling continuous action experts to VLM backbones degrades semantic knowledge and training dynamics. However, their insulation technique treats the VLM backbone somewhat uniformly. Different VLM layers encode qualitatively different information (low-level visual features, semantic concepts, task-level reasoning), and blindly insulating all layers may be overly conservative, sacrificing useful plasticity, or insufficiently targeted, leaving critical semantic layers vulnerable to corruption during VLA fine-tuning. Proposed Method: We propose Layer-wise Relevance-Guided Selective Insulation (LRSI), which uses gradient-based layer relevance scores computed on held-out VLM benchmarks to identify semantically critical layers before VLA training begins. Only layers with high relevance scores for preserving downstream language and visual understanding are frozen or heavily regularized via elastic weight consolidation, while less critical layers remain plastic for action-relevant adaptation. A small router network dynamically gates gradient flow through boundary layers. Planned Experiments: (1) Benchmark semantic knowledge retention across VLM tasks (VQA, MMLU-vision) vs. standard insulation and full fine-tuning baselines; (2) Robot manipulation success rates on seen and novel task categories using simulated (RLBench) and real environments; (3) Ablations varying the relevance threshold; (4) Training convergence speed comparison; (5) Analysis of which layer types are identified as critical across different VLM architectures (LLaVA, Qwen-VL).

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Fine-tuning: When and What to Insulate Across Training Curriculum
description:
Problem: The knowledge insulation paper treats VLM backbone protection as a static design choice applied uniformly throughout training. However, different training phases may benefit from different insulation strategies—early training may require more backbone flexibility to align action representations, while later stages should preserve semantic knowledge to enable generalization. A fixed insulation scheme may sub-optimally trade off adaptation speed against knowledge retention.

Method: We propose Dynamic Insulation Scheduling (DIS), which learns or schedules layer-wise insulation coefficients across training stages. Specifically, we parameterize per-layer insulation gates as functions of training progress and task diversity metrics. We explore three variants: (1) annealed insulation that progressively freezes backbone layers as training matures, (2) curriculum-aware insulation that increases backbone coupling when training on novel semantic categories requiring knowledge transfer, and (3) gradient-magnitude-triggered insulation that automatically detects when action expert updates begin corrupting VLM representations.

Experiments: We evaluate on LIBERO, OpenX-Embodiment, and a held-out generalization benchmark with novel object categories. Metrics include: task success rate, training convergence speed, VLM semantic probe accuracy throughout training, and zero-shot generalization to unseen instructions. We compare against static insulation baselines from the anchor paper, full fine-tuning, and LoRA approaches, ablating each DIS variant to isolate contributions of dynamic scheduling.

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Fine-tuning: When to Thaw and What to Update
description:
Problem: Knowledge Insulation work shows that naively coupling a continuous action expert to a VLM backbone degrades pretrained semantic knowledge and slows training. However, static insulation strategies (permanently freezing or gating backbone layers) may be overly conservative, preventing the backbone from adapting useful task-specific visual features needed for precise manipulation. A principled dynamic freezing schedule could balance knowledge preservation with necessary adaptation.

Proposed Method: We propose Adaptive Thaw Scheduling (ATS), which monitors per-layer Fisher Information estimates and gradient signal-to-noise ratios during VLA training to automatically determine which backbone layers should be unfrozen and when. Early training phases maintain full insulation; as the action expert converges, ATS selectively unfreezes layers with high task-relevant Fisher Information scores, allowing targeted backbone adaptation without catastrophic forgetting. We additionally introduce a knowledge retention regularizer that penalizes drift in VLM output distributions on held-out vision-language tasks during robot policy training.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on standard robot manipulation suites (LIBERO, OpenVLA splits) comparing ATS against static insulation, full fine-tuning, and LoRA baselines. (2) Measure knowledge retention via VQA and captioning probes throughout training. (3) Evaluate generalization to novel object categories and language instructions. (4) Ablate Fisher threshold hyperparameters and thaw timing schedules. (5) Profile inference latency to ensure real-time viability.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Fine-tuning: A Neuron-Level Analysis of Knowledge Preservation vs. Motor Skill Acquisition
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs currently treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, applying uniform freezing or gradient isolation strategies. However, different layers and attention heads within the VLM encode qualitatively different knowledge—early layers capture low-level visual features, middle layers encode semantic concepts, and later layers handle task-specific reasoning. A blanket insulation strategy may over-constrain motor-relevant representations while under-protecting semantic ones, limiting the VLA's ability to ground language instructions in motor primitives.

Proposed Method: We introduce Neuron-Selective Knowledge Insulation (NSKI), which uses gradient attribution and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to identify, per layer, which neurons encode transferable semantic knowledge versus those that benefit from motor adaptation. We maintain a frozen 'semantic anchor' copy of the VLM and apply layer-wise adaptive learning rates guided by a knowledge drift penalty that is proportional to each layer's semantic importance score. A lightweight router module learns which representations to pull from the frozen versus adapting stream.

Experiments: (1) Systematic ablation across 6 VLM architectures comparing NSKI against uniform freezing and the baseline insulation from the anchor paper. (2) Evaluation on LIBERO, Calvin, and real robot manipulation benchmarks measuring task success, generalization to novel object categories, and instruction following. (3) Probing classifiers to quantify retained semantic knowledge per layer throughout training. (4) Training efficiency analysis measuring wall-clock convergence.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge Across Sequential Robot Task Acquisition
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation addresses degradation during initial VLA training, deployed robots must continually acquire new tasks without catastrophically forgetting previously learned ones or eroding the semantic knowledge inherited from the VLM backbone. The interaction between continual learning dynamics and VLM knowledge preservation remains unexplored. Proposed Method: We introduce Semantics-Preserving Continual VLA (SP-CVLA), which combines knowledge insulation with a dynamic layer importance scoring mechanism. Using Fisher Information Matrix estimates computed over the VLM's language-grounding layers, we identify and selectively freeze the most semantically critical parameters during each new task acquisition phase. For the action expert, we employ low-rank task-specific adapter modules (LoRA) that expand capacity without disturbing backbone representations. A semantic drift metric—measuring cosine similarity between frozen reference embeddings and current representations on a fixed probe dataset—serves as a regularization signal during training. Experiments: We evaluate on a sequential 10-task robot manipulation benchmark using OpenVLA and π0-style architectures, measuring (1) forward transfer to new tasks, (2) backward transfer/forgetting on prior tasks, (3) VLM semantic retention via visual question-answering probes, and (4) wall-clock training efficiency. Ablations compare full fine-tuning, EWC, PackNet, naive insulation, and SP-CVLA across 3 robot platforms.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Fine-Tuning: Identifying and Preserving Semantic Knowledge Reservoirs
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation techniques protect VLM backbones during VLA training, they apply uniform protection across all layers. However, semantic knowledge (object recognition, spatial reasoning, task semantics) is distributed heterogeneously across transformer layers, with some layers acting as critical 'knowledge reservoirs' while others are more adaptation-friendly. Naively freezing everything wastes representational capacity; naively fine-tuning everything destroys critical knowledge. Proposed Method: We introduce Semantic Reservoir Identification (SRI), a method that probes each transformer layer's contribution to downstream semantic tasks (VQA, object grounding, spatial reasoning) using lightweight diagnostic classifiers before VLA training begins. Layers scoring above a semantic importance threshold are selectively frozen or trained with heavily reduced learning rates, while layers with low semantic importance receive standard fine-tuning. We combine this with the existing knowledge insulation framework, replacing uniform backbone treatment with layer-wise adaptive training schedules. Additionally, we propose a dynamic threshold that relaxes layer freezing as training progresses, allowing gradual semantic adaptation. Experiments: We evaluate on SimplerEnv and real robot manipulation tasks (BridgeV2, OXE subsets) measuring: (1) task success rate, (2) semantic knowledge retention via VQA benchmarks throughout training, (3) training convergence speed, and (4) out-of-distribution generalization with novel object categories, comparing against full fine-tuning, uniform insulation, and LoRA baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Tasks
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation during VLA training preserves VLM semantic knowledge, a single global insulation strategy may be suboptimal across diverse robot tasks—some tasks (e.g., semantic instruction following) benefit more from preserved VLM knowledge, while others (e.g., precise manipulation) require deeper fine-tuning of visual representations. A principled method for task-adaptive, layer-selective insulation is missing. Proposed Method: We introduce ATLAS (Adaptive Task-Layer Insulation Strategy), which automatically identifies which VLM layers to insulate versus fine-tune based on two signals: (1) a per-layer semantic drift metric measured by cosine similarity of layer activations between the base VLM and the VLA during training, and (2) task-conditioned importance scores derived from gradient magnitude statistics across heterogeneous task demonstrations. ATLAS uses these signals to dynamically assign per-layer insulation coefficients that are updated periodically during training, rather than applying uniform insulation across all backbone layers. Experiments: We evaluate on LIBERO benchmark suites (spatial, object, goal, long-horizon), Open-X-Embodiment multi-robot splits, and a new benchmark mixing language-heavy and precision-heavy tasks. We compare against full fine-tuning, uniform insulation (baseline from anchor paper), and LoRA-based adaptation, measuring training convergence speed, task success rates, and semantic knowledge retention via VQA probing tasks on held-out visual question datasets.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs has been studied primarily for a single robot platform, but different robot morphologies (manipulators, humanoids, mobile robots) impose vastly different action space dimensionalities and control frequencies. It remains unclear which VLM layers are most susceptible to catastrophic forgetting during action expert integration, and whether optimal insulation strategies transfer across morphologies. Method: We propose MorphAdapt, a structured layer-sensitivity analysis framework that (1) computes per-layer semantic knowledge retention scores using probing classifiers on VLM benchmarks during VLA fine-tuning, (2) identifies morphology-specific 'critical layers' whose representations degrade most under action expert coupling, and (3) applies gradient-scaled selective freezing—partially freezing critical layers with learnable per-layer retention coefficients rather than binary freeze/unfreeze decisions. This allows dynamic trade-offs between plasticity and knowledge preservation tuned per morphology. Experiments: We train VLAs on three robot morphologies (7-DOF arm, 23-DOF humanoid, mobile manipulator) using diffusion action experts, comparing full fine-tuning, full insulation, and MorphAdapt against standardized semantic retention benchmarks (VQA, referring expression) and robot task success rates across 15 manipulation and navigation tasks. We analyze cross-morphology transferability of discovered critical layer patterns and validate on a held-out legged locomotion platform.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Fine-Tuning: When to Insulate, When to Adapt
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, applying uniform insulation strategies. However, different VLM layers encode qualitatively different knowledge — lower layers capture perceptual features while higher layers encode semantic/reasoning capabilities. Naive full-backbone insulation may unnecessarily restrict task-specific visual grounding needed for manipulation, while full fine-tuning destroys semantic knowledge. We lack principled methods for identifying which layers to insulate versus adapt during VLA training. Proposed Method: We introduce 'LayerProbe-VLA,' a diagnostic framework that measures per-layer knowledge retention (via probing classifiers on VLM benchmarks) and task-relevance (via gradient signal analysis) throughout VLA training. Based on these measurements, we develop an adaptive layer-wise insulation schedule that automatically determines insulation coefficients per layer, allowing semantic layers to remain frozen while permitting controlled adaptation in perceptual layers. We further propose a curriculum: begin with full insulation, then progressively release lower layers as action expert training stabilizes. Experiments: We evaluate on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures across (1) real robot manipulation tasks requiring visual grounding, (2) VLM benchmark retention (VQA, spatial reasoning), (3) training convergence speed, and (4) out-of-distribution generalization, comparing against uniform insulation baselines and LoRA-based approaches.

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Fine-tuning: When and What to Insulate During Continual Robot Skill Acquisition
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs focuses on preserving VLM backbone knowledge during initial action expert integration, but continual learning of new robot skills (e.g., sequential task acquisition across different environments) introduces a distinct challenge: naively fine-tuning the entire VLA on new skills causes catastrophic forgetting of both semantic VLM knowledge and previously learned motor skills. Static insulation strategies may be overly conservative, preventing beneficial plasticity when learning genuinely novel perceptual-motor mappings. Method: We propose Dynamic Insulation Scheduling (DIS), which automatically determines per-layer freeze/unfreeze decisions throughout continual VLA training using gradient signal-to-noise ratios and representational similarity analysis (RSA) between current and original VLM layer activations. Layers exhibiting high semantic drift (measured by RSA) are re-insulated, while layers with low task-relevant gradient signal are frozen to conserve compute. We additionally introduce a lightweight skill-specific adapter bank that absorbs task-specific adaptations without polluting shared backbone representations. Experiments: We evaluate on a continual learning benchmark comprising 10 sequential manipulation tasks in simulation (RLBench) and 5 real-robot tasks, measuring forward transfer, backward transfer, semantic retention (VQA accuracy), and inference latency. Ablations compare static insulation, EWC, LoRA, and DIS variants.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Vision-Language Backbones
description: Problem: Knowledge Insulation (KI) in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolith—either updating all layers or protecting them uniformly. However, different VLM layers encode different levels of abstraction (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantic reasoning), and the optimal insulation strategy may vary by layer depth, modality, and task complexity. Blindly freezing all backbone parameters may sacrifice task-relevant plasticity, while full fine-tuning destroys semantic knowledge as shown in the anchor paper. Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Adaptive Knowledge Insulation (LAKI), a method that learns per-layer insulation coefficients during VLA training. Specifically, we add lightweight scalar gates (initialized to 1.0) to each transformer layer's residual stream, regularized to stay near 1.0 (preserving knowledge) but allowed to decay when gradient signals indicate task-relevant updates are needed. We combine this with a probing-based diagnostic that measures semantic retention per layer throughout training. This allows the model to selectively update task-critical layers while insulating semantically rich ones. Experiments: We evaluate LAKI on Open-X-Embodiment benchmarks and simulated manipulation tasks (LIBERO, MetaWorld), measuring (1) downstream task success rates, (2) semantic retention via VQA probing at each layer, (3) training convergence speed, and (4) cross-task generalization, comparing against full fine-tuning, uniform KI, and LoRA baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Matters
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, applying uniform insulation strategies. However, different layers of a VLM encode qualitatively different knowledge (low-level visual features, mid-level semantic concepts, high-level reasoning), and robotic control tasks may benefit from fine-tuning some layers while preserving others. The optimal insulation granularity remains unexplored.

Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Selective Insulation (LSI), a principled approach that identifies which VLM layers to freeze, partially update, or fully fine-tune during VLA training. We use gradient-based importance scores (Fisher information approximation) computed on a small set of manipulation demonstrations to rank layers by their contribution to task performance vs. knowledge preservation. We then apply a soft insulation schedule that gradually unfreezes layers from top to bottom as training progresses, combined with knowledge distillation losses only on identified high-level semantic layers.

Experiments: (1) Compare LSI against uniform insulation and full fine-tuning on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures across 8 manipulation tasks in simulation (RLBench) and 4 real-robot tasks. (2) Measure semantic knowledge retention via VQA benchmarks throughout training. (3) Ablate freezing schedules, distillation weights, and layer selection criteria. (4) Evaluate sample efficiency and wall-clock training time.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Models: When and What to Insulate Across Diverse Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLA models has been studied primarily for a single robot embodiment and action space. However, deployed robots vary dramatically in morphology (arms, quadrupeds, dexterous hands), and it is unclear whether the same insulation strategy preserves VLM knowledge equally well across embodiments with different action dimensionalities, control frequencies, and semantic grounding requirements. A blanket insulation strategy may over-freeze layers beneficial for motor adaptation or under-protect layers critical for language grounding in novel embodiments. Method: We propose Morphology-Adaptive Selective Insulation (MASI), which uses gradient-flow analysis and representational similarity metrics (CKA) during early training to automatically identify which VLM layers are most vulnerable to semantic degradation for a given embodiment's action expert. MASI then applies layer-wise insulation strength proportional to measured degradation risk, rather than applying uniform insulation. We also introduce a lightweight probing benchmark measuring VLM semantic retention (VQA accuracy, zero-shot classification) continuously during VLA fine-tuning. Experiments: We train VLAs across four embodiments (Franka arm, Allegro hand, Unitree quadruped, bi-manual setup) using π0-style flow-matching action experts, comparing uniform insulation, no insulation, and MASI. Metrics include task success rate, training convergence speed, and semantic retention scores, evaluating generalization to unseen instructions and objects.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Tasks
description:
Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs demonstrates that protecting VLM backbone knowledge during action expert training improves generalization. However, the optimal insulation strategy is treated as uniform across all layers and tasks. Different robot manipulation tasks (fine motor control vs. coarse navigation vs. semantic reasoning) likely benefit from different layer-wise insulation patterns — some tasks need deeper semantic adaptation while others need only shallow motor fine-tuning. Naively applying full insulation may under-adapt for complex tasks; no insulation over-corrupts pretrained knowledge.

Proposed Method: We propose Task-Adaptive Gradient Insulation (TAGI), which learns per-layer insulation masks conditioned on task complexity metrics (semantic diversity of instructions, action space dimensionality, training data volume). We parameterize insulation as a differentiable soft gate per transformer layer, jointly optimized via a bi-level objective: inner loop minimizes control loss, outer loop maximizes retention of VLM probing accuracy on held-out vision-language benchmarks. We additionally introduce a task-complexity estimator that predicts optimal insulation depth from task metadata alone, enabling zero-shot insulation policy selection for new tasks.

Experiments: (1) Ablate TAGI vs. uniform insulation on LIBERO, RLBench, and Open-X-Embodiment subsets across task categories. (2) Measure VLM knowledge retention via VQA probing after adaptation. (3) Evaluate generalization to unseen objects/instructions. (4) Analyze learned insulation masks to reveal interpretable layer-function specialization patterns.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Diverse Manipulation Tasks
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation technique proposed for VLAs applies a uniform strategy to protect VLM backbone knowledge during action expert training. However, different layers of a VLM encode qualitatively different knowledge (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantic reasoning), and different manipulation tasks may benefit from selectively preserving or adapting specific layer subsets. A one-size-fits-all insulation approach may over-constrain adaptation for tasks requiring novel visual grounding or under-constrain it for tasks where semantic drift causes performance degradation. Proposed Method: We introduce Task-Adaptive Selective Insulation (TASI), which automatically identifies which VLM layers to insulate versus fine-tune based on task-specific signals. We use gradient-based importance scores computed on a small held-out task dataset to rank layer sensitivity, then apply a threshold policy to freeze insensitive layers while allowing targeted adaptation in semantically relevant ones. A lightweight meta-learning outer loop learns initialization biases for the threshold policy across task families. Planned Experiments: (1) Benchmark TASI against uniform insulation and full fine-tuning on 12 manipulation tasks spanning semantic diversity (language-conditioned, novel object generalization, multi-step planning); (2) Ablate layer-wise freezing patterns and correlate with probing classifiers measuring semantic knowledge retention; (3) Measure inference latency and training convergence speed; (4) Test zero-shot transfer to unseen task categories. Expected outcome: TASI achieves better generalization than uniform insulation while maintaining comparable inference efficiency.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for Continual VLA Adaptation: Preserving Semantic Knowledge Across Task Domains
description:
Problem: Knowledge insulation addresses VLM backbone degradation during initial VLA training, but robots must continually adapt to new task domains (e.g., kitchen→warehouse→surgical) without catastrophic forgetting of previously learned semantic and motor skills. Naively fine-tuning VLAs on new domains destroys both VLM semantic knowledge and previously acquired action competencies simultaneously, compounding the insulation problem across time.

Proposed Method: We propose Elastic Knowledge Insulation (EKI), a continual learning framework for VLAs that dynamically identifies and protects task-critical parameter subspaces across both the VLM backbone and action expert. EKI computes Fisher Information Matrices over VLM semantic layers and action expert layers separately, maintaining distinct importance scores for semantic versus motor knowledge. A dual-pathway EWC-style penalty prevents semantic knowledge erosion while allowing motor skill plasticity, combined with a small episodic replay buffer storing compressed task-boundary demonstrations. We further introduce a knowledge drift metric—measuring VLM embedding shift on a fixed semantic probe set—as an online signal for adaptive regularization strength.

Experiments: We evaluate on sequential adaptation across 5 robot manipulation domains (FurnitureBench→RLBench→BridgeV2→surgical simulation→outdoor manipulation), measuring: per-task success rates, VLM semantic probe accuracy, forward transfer, and backward transfer. Ablations compare against naive fine-tuning, standard EWC, LoRA-based approaches, and the original knowledge insulation baseline without continual learning components.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge Across Sequential Task Acquisition
description: Problem: When VLA models are deployed in the real world, robots must continuously acquire new manipulation skills without forgetting previously learned ones. Current knowledge insulation techniques focus on preserving VLM knowledge during initial VLA training, but the continual learning setting—where new tasks arrive sequentially—remains unexplored. Naively fine-tuning on new tasks catastrophically forgets both VLM semantic knowledge and previously learned motor skills simultaneously. Method: We propose Knowledge-Insulated Continual VLA (KI-CVLA), which extends knowledge insulation principles to sequential task learning. We identify that different transformer layers encode semantic knowledge (early/mid layers) versus task-specific motor programs (later layers and action expert), and design a dynamic layer-selective update strategy: semantic layers are frozen or updated with minimal LoRA rank, while action-relevant layers receive full gradient flow. We introduce a knowledge retention score that monitors VLM semantic capabilities online and triggers protective freezing when degradation is detected. A task-specific routing mechanism in the action expert head enables skill isolation without parameter explosion. Experiments: We evaluate on a 10-task sequential manipulation benchmark (RLBench + real robot tasks), measuring: (1) forward transfer to new tasks, (2) backward transfer/forgetting of old tasks, (3) VLM semantic retention via VQA probing throughout training, and (4) wall-clock inference speed. Baselines include EWC, PackNet, naive fine-tuning, and full knowledge insulation with task-ID conditioning.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge Across Sequential Robot Task Acquisition
description:
Problem: VLA models face catastrophic forgetting when sequentially fine-tuned on new robot tasks — each new skill acquisition degrades previously learned capabilities. While knowledge insulation addresses degradation during initial VLA training, no principled method exists for continual VLA learning that preserves both semantic VLM knowledge and previously acquired motor skills simultaneously.

Proposed Method: We introduce Gradient-Sensitive Insulation Masks (GSIM), a continual learning framework for VLAs that dynamically identifies and freezes parameter subsets critical to both semantic knowledge and prior task performance. Building on knowledge insulation insights, we compute task-specific Fisher information matrices to identify 'doubly-sensitive' parameters — those important to both VLM representations and previously learned action distributions. These parameters receive strong regularization penalties during new task acquisition, while action expert heads are task-specific and modular. A lightweight task-routing mechanism selects appropriate heads at inference time.

Experiments: (1) Sequential fine-tuning on 10 diverse manipulation tasks in simulation (RLBench), measuring forward transfer and backward transfer. (2) Comparison against EWC, PackNet, and naive fine-tuning baselines. (3) Ablation of Fisher computation strategies (semantic-only, motor-only, joint). (4) Real-robot evaluation on 5 sequential tasks measuring semantic grounding retention via VQA probing after each task addition. (5) Inference latency benchmarking of routing overhead.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Models: When and What to Insulate Across Heterogeneous Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation technique proposed for VLAs assumes a monolithic fine-tuning strategy, but different robot morphologies (manipulators, quadrupeds, humanoids) likely require different degrees of VLM backbone modification. Some tasks demand heavy semantic grounding (language-conditioned manipulation), while others demand low-level proprioceptive control (locomotion). A single insulation strategy may over-constrain or under-constrain adaptation depending on the domain, leading to suboptimal trade-offs between knowledge preservation and task-specific adaptation. Proposed Method: We introduce Morphology-Adaptive Selective Insulation (MASI), a method that learns per-layer insulation masks conditioned on task/morphology type. Using a differentiable binary gate trained via a small held-out validation set, MASI discovers which VLM layers benefit from freezing versus fine-tuning for each robot class. We additionally propose an insulation scheduler that gradually relaxes frozen layers as training progresses, allowing controlled semantic drift. Experiments: (1) Evaluate MASI across three robot morphologies (arm, quadruped, humanoid) on simulation benchmarks (RLBench, IsaacGym, HumanoidBench); (2) Compare against full fine-tuning, uniform insulation, and random freezing baselines using language generalization probes; (3) Measure training convergence speed and zero-shot language generalization to novel instructions; (4) Ablate gating granularity (per-layer vs per-attention-head vs per-module).

title: Selective Layer Freezing for Modality-Specific Knowledge Preservation in VLA Fine-Tuning
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs treats the VLM backbone as a monolithic entity to protect, but different layers encode different types of knowledge (low-level visual features, semantic concepts, language grounding). Naively freezing or regularizing the entire backbone may over-constrain action-relevant representations while under-protecting semantic knowledge critical for generalization. Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-wise Knowledge Importance Scoring (LKIS), a technique that probes each transformer layer's contribution to semantic tasks (VQA, captioning, language grounding) before VLA training begins. Using these importance scores, we construct a per-layer freezing schedule: highly semantic layers receive stronger gradient insulation (full freeze or high regularization penalty), while layers encoding lower-level visual features receive partial or no constraints, allowing them to adapt to the robot's visual domain. We further propose a dynamic unfreezing curriculum that gradually relaxes constraints on semantic layers as training progresses, guided by monitored semantic probe accuracy. Experiments: We evaluate on LIBERO and Open-X-Embodiment benchmarks, measuring (1) task success rate across seen and unseen environments, (2) semantic knowledge retention via held-out VQA probes, (3) training convergence speed, and (4) comparison against uniform insulation baselines and LoRA-based approaches. We ablate across different backbone sizes (7B, 13B) and action expert types (diffusion, flow matching).

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When to Insulate, When to Finetune
description: Problem: The knowledge insulation technique proposed for VLAs applies a uniform strategy across the entire VLM backbone. However, different transformer layers encode qualitatively different information—lower layers capture low-level visual features while higher layers encode semantic concepts and task-relevant abstractions. A blanket insulation policy may over-constrain semantically relevant adaptation or under-protect critical knowledge layers, leaving performance on the table. Method: We propose LayerAdapt-VLA, a method that learns a per-layer adaptation schedule during VLA training using gradient signal analysis. Specifically, we compute layer-wise knowledge retention scores (measuring KL divergence from the pretrained VLM's internal representations on held-out vision-language tasks) and action-relevance scores (measuring gradient magnitude flowing from the action expert into each layer). These dual scores drive a dynamic binary gate per layer that decides whether to insulate or allow fine-tuning at each training stage. We also explore a soft interpolation variant using learned mixing coefficients. Experiments: We evaluate on OpenVLA and π0-style architectures across (1) standard manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO, RLBench), (2) out-of-distribution generalization (novel objects/instructions), and (3) vision-language task retention (VQA, captioning). We compare against full fine-tuning, full insulation, LoRA, and layer-wise LR scaling baselines, measuring sample efficiency, inference latency, and semantic knowledge preservation.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Adaptation: When and Where to Insulate Across Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs demonstrates that protecting VLM backbone knowledge during action expert integration improves generalization. However, the paper treats insulation as a uniform architectural decision applied globally. An open question is whether different VLM layers encode qualitatively different types of knowledge (low-level visual features vs. semantic reasoning vs. spatial relations), and whether optimal insulation strategies should vary across robot embodiments (arms, quadrupeds, humanoids) with different action spaces and sensor modalities. Method: We propose Layer-Adaptive Insulation (LAI), which learns per-layer insulation coefficients during VLA training using a lightweight meta-objective that measures downstream semantic knowledge retention (via frozen VLM probe accuracy on held-out VQA tasks) alongside task performance. LAI uses differentiable gating on gradient flow per transformer layer, allowing the model to discover which layers to insulate vs. fine-tune for each embodiment. We additionally introduce a cross-embodiment knowledge transfer protocol where insulation masks learned on one robot are transferred to new morphologies as initialization. Experiments: We train on three robot platforms (Franka arm, Unitree quadruped, Fourier humanoid) across 50+ tasks, measuring (1) final task success, (2) VQA knowledge retention, (3) sample efficiency, and (4) cross-embodiment transfer versus uniform insulation baselines from the anchor paper. We expect LAI to reveal that later VLM layers require stronger insulation across embodiments while early visual layers benefit from fine-tuning.

title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Continual Learning: Preserving Semantic Knowledge Across Sequential Task Acquisition
description: Problem: While knowledge insulation addresses catastrophic forgetting during initial VLA training, robots deployed in the real world must continuously acquire new manipulation skills without forgetting previously learned ones. Standard continual learning approaches ignore the heterogeneous knowledge distribution across VLM backbone layers, leading to unnecessary computation and suboptimal knowledge preservation. Proposed Method: We propose Semantic-Aware Continual VLA (SAC-VLA), which dynamically identifies and selectively freezes layers with high semantic knowledge density (measured via representational similarity to the original VLM using CKA scores) while allowing plasticity in layers that predominantly encode task-specific motor primitives. A lightweight importance scoring module runs online before each new task, producing a binary freeze mask per layer. A small episodic memory buffer stores prototypical embeddings from prior tasks for drift detection. When semantic drift exceeds a threshold in previously-frozen layers, elastic weight consolidation is applied locally rather than globally, reducing compute overhead by ~60%. Experiments: We evaluate on a sequential 10-task manipulation benchmark (MetaWorld + RLBench) comparing against EWC, PackNet, LoRA-based continual methods, and the knowledge insulation baseline. Metrics include backward transfer, forward transfer, inference latency, and VQA accuracy on held-out semantic probes after each sequential task. Ablations examine freeze mask granularity and episodic buffer size.
