title: Selective Layer Freezing for VLA Knowledge Preservation: A Gradient-Based Importance Analysis Across Heterogeneous Robot Tasks
description:
Problem: The knowledge insulation paper demonstrates that naive VLA training harms VLM backbone knowledge, but proposes a uniform insulation strategy. In practice, different robot tasks (manipulation, navigation, dexterous grasping) likely require different amounts of semantic versus motor knowledge from different VLM layers. A one-size-fits-all insulation strategy may under-preserve task-critical semantic features or over-constrain layers that could beneficially adapt.

Proposed Method: We develop a task-adaptive layer importance scoring method that uses gradient-based attribution (Fisher information or EWC-style diagonal Hessian approximation) to identify which VLM layers contribute most to semantic generalization versus motor control for each task family. We then apply a continuous, task-conditional freezing schedule where insulation strength varies per layer and per task domain, rather than binary freeze/unfreeze. A lightweight meta-learned gating network predicts per-layer insulation coefficients given task embeddings, trained jointly with the VLA.

Experiments: (1) Measure per-layer gradient norms and Fisher information across diverse robot task categories on Open-X-Embodiment. (2) Compare fixed insulation, random layer freezing, and our adaptive method on cross-task generalization benchmarks. (3) Ablate gating network architectures and scoring methods. (4) Evaluate zero-shot transfer to unseen task categories. Expected outcome: adaptive insulation outperforms uniform insulation by 15-25% on novel task generalization while maintaining inference speed.

title: Selective Layer Freezing via Gradient Sensitivity Analysis for VLA Knowledge Preservation
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs currently applies uniform backbone protection strategies, but different VLM layers contribute heterogeneously to semantic knowledge versus motor control learning. Indiscriminate freezing wastes representational capacity, while full fine-tuning degrades semantic knowledge. We need a principled, layer-wise approach to preserving knowledge where it matters most while enabling adaptation where beneficial. Proposed Method: We introduce Gradient Sensitivity-Aware Freezing (GSAF), which analyzes per-layer gradient norms and Fisher information during early VLA training to identify which backbone layers are most semantically critical versus most amenable to action-relevant adaptation. We then apply a dynamic, layer-specific learning rate schedule and selective LoRA insertion: high-sensitivity layers receive near-zero learning rates and no LoRA, mid-sensitivity layers receive small LoRA ranks, and low-sensitivity layers receive larger LoRA ranks with standard learning rates. The sensitivity profiles are computed once on a small held-out semantic benchmark before robot training begins. Experiments: We train on the Open-X-Embodiment dataset with a PaliGemma-based VLA backbone, comparing GSAF against uniform freezing, full fine-tuning, and the knowledge insulation baseline from the anchor paper. Evaluation metrics include: task success rates on seen/unseen tasks, semantic benchmark retention (VQA, captioning), training convergence speed, and cross-embodiment generalization. We ablate sensitivity metrics and update frequency.

title: Selective Layer Freezing via Gradient Sensitivity Analysis for VLA Fine-tuning Across Heterogeneous Robot Morphologies
description: Problem: When adapting a single pretrained VLA model to robots with fundamentally different morphologies (manipulators, quadrupeds, humanoids), naive fine-tuning either catastrophically forgets semantic VLM knowledge or fails to specialize sufficiently for each embodiment. Knowledge insulation helps preserve VLM knowledge but applies a uniform strategy regardless of which layers actually encode embodiment-specific vs. semantically-rich representations. Method: We propose Morphology-Aware Selective Insulation (MASI), which automatically identifies layer-wise gradient sensitivity profiles by measuring how gradients flow through the VLM backbone when exposed to each robot embodiment's action distribution. Layers showing high cross-morphology gradient interference are frozen or insulated, while layers showing low interference are selectively fine-tuned per embodiment via lightweight LoRA adapters. A shared semantic core is preserved via the insulation technique from the anchor paper, while per-morphology adapters handle embodiment-specific motor control patterns. Experiments: We train on three embodiments (Franka arm, Unitree quadruped, Agility Cassie biped) using a shared π0-style backbone, measuring (1) task success rates per embodiment, (2) VLM semantic retention via visual QA benchmarks, (3) training convergence speed, and (4) cross-embodiment transfer to a held-out robot. We compare against full fine-tuning, uniform insulation, and standard LoRA baselines.

title: Selective Layer Freezing Schedules for VLA Fine-tuning: When and What to Insulate During Continual Task Adaptation
description: Problem: Knowledge insulation in VLAs currently treats backbone preservation as a static design choice applied uniformly during training. However, different VLM layers encode different levels of semantic abstraction, and the optimal insulation strategy likely varies across training stages and task types. Naively freezing all backbone layers limits plasticity for novel manipulation tasks, while full fine-tuning degrades semantic priors—a dynamic middle ground remains unexplored. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Insulation Scheduling (AIS), a method that dynamically modulates per-layer learning rates and freeze/unfreeze decisions during VLA training based on two signals: (1) layer-wise gradient signal-to-noise ratios indicating whether a layer is receiving meaningful task-relevant updates, and (2) semantic drift metrics measuring KL divergence between current and pretrained VLM token distributions. AIS periodically probes each layer and adjusts insulation strength accordingly, allowing early semantic layers to remain frozen while permitting targeted adaptation in mid-to-late layers when task demands require it. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) standard manipulation benchmarks from prior VLA work, (2) cross-domain generalization to novel object categories, and (3) continual learning across sequential task streams. Ablations compare static insulation, full fine-tuning, LoRA, and AIS variants. Primary metrics include task success rate, knowledge retention on VQA benchmarks, and wall-clock training efficiency.

title: Selective Layer Freezing via Representational Drift Analysis for VLA Fine-tuning
description: Problem: Knowledge Insulating VLAs demonstrates that adding action experts degrades pretrained VLM semantic knowledge, but applies insulation uniformly across the backbone. Different VLM layers encode different levels of abstraction (low-level visual features vs. high-level semantics), and uniform insulation may unnecessarily constrain layers that could beneficially adapt while over-protecting layers that are stable. We lack principled methods to identify which specific layers are most vulnerable to semantic degradation during VLA training. Proposed Method: We introduce RepDrift-VLA, a technique that measures layer-wise representational drift during VLA fine-tuning using centered kernel alignment (CKA) between pretrained and fine-tuned layer activations on a frozen semantic probe dataset. We use these drift profiles to construct adaptive per-layer learning rate schedules and selective LoRA ranks, applying stronger insulation only to high-drift semantically-critical layers while allowing lower layers to adapt freely. This replaces blanket backbone freezing with a data-driven, layer-specific insulation strategy. Planned Experiments: (1) Profile drift across layers for multiple VLA architectures (pi0, OpenVLA) with diffusion/flow-matching action experts; (2) Compare RepDrift-VLA against uniform freezing, full fine-tuning, and standard knowledge insulation on Open-X-Embodiment benchmarks; (3) Measure semantic retention via VQA probes, training convergence speed, and sim-to-real transfer on a manipulation task suite; (4) Ablate CKA threshold sensitivity and LoRA rank allocation strategies.
